events.title: Lower Palaeolithic: earliest stone tools
events.summary: The earliest stone tools in India — hand-axes, cleavers and choppers of the Lower Palaeolithic — come from sites such as the Soan valley, Attirampakkam, Bhimbetka and Nagarjunakonda.
events.detail:
People lived as hunter-gatherers using tools of quartzite. There was no pottery, farming or metal. The Palaeolithic is divided into Lower (hand-axes), Middle (flakes) and Upper (blades and burins) phases.

Robert Bruce Foote found the first Palaeolithic hand-axe in India at Pallavaram near Madras in 1863. Bhimbetka (Madhya Pradesh) has rock shelters with paintings and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
causes: Early humans spreading across the subcontinent.
outcomes: Middle and Upper Palaeolithic tool traditions followed.
events.yearHook: From about 5 lakh (500,000) years ago, maybe earlier. The Stone Age is "Old → Middle → New": Palaeolithic → Mesolithic (about 9000 BCE) → Neolithic (about 7000 BCE).
facts: John Lubbock coined the words Palaeolithic and Neolithic (1865).
V.S. Wakankar discovered the Bhimbetka rock shelters (1957).
Paleolithic sites also include Attirampakkam (Tamil Nadu), Hunsgi, Didwana and the Belan valley.
events.before: Human ancestors evolved in Africa and spread across Asia. In India the oldest tools are hand-axes and cleavers of quartzite. There was no farming, pottery or metal; people hunted, fished and gathered.
events.after: The last Ice Age ended about 10,000 years ago. A warmer, wetter climate brought more plants and small animals, and people made tiny tools: the **Mesolithic** (next event).
events.today: **Bhimbetka** (MP) rock shelters are a UNESCO site. **Attirampakkam** (near Chennai) has tools about 1.5 million years old. In AP, **Nagarjunakonda** and the Kurnool caves have Palaeolithic tools.
events.mnemonic: Palaeolithic tools by phase "H-F-B": Lower = Hand-axes, Middle = Flakes, Upper = Blades and burins. Foote found the first hand-axe at Pallavaram (1863).

events.title: Mesolithic microliths & Bhimbetka art
events.summary: In the Mesolithic (Middle Stone Age, from about 9000 BCE) people use tiny stone tools called microliths and begin to domesticate animals.
events.detail: Sites include Bagor (Rajasthan) and Adamgarh (Madhya Pradesh), which give the earliest evidence of domesticated animals; Bhimbetka paintings show hunting and dancing. The climate became warmer after the Ice Age.
causes: Warmer climate after the last Ice Age.
outcomes: Led to farming in the Neolithic.
events.yearHook: About 9000 BCE: right after the last Ice Age ended (about 10,000 years ago).
facts: Mesolithic sites: Bagor (Rajasthan, the largest), Adamgarh (MP), Sarai Nahar Rai, Mahadaha and Lekhahia (UP), Langhnaj (Gujarat).
events.before: The **Old Stone Age** hunters (from about 5 lakh years ago) used big stone tools. When the Ice Age ended, forests and grasslands spread and big game moved away.
events.after: People began to tame animals and, later, to grow crops. The first farming village of the subcontinent was **Mehrgarh** (about 7000 BCE, next event).
events.today: The Bhimbetka paintings of hunting and dancing can still be seen in Raisen district, MP.
events.mnemonic: "Bagor is Biggest; Adamgarh And Bagor have the first tamed Animals". Microlith = micro (small) + lith (stone).

examAngle.point: Giddalur (Giddaluru, Prakasam district) is a known microlithic tool site.
examAngle.context: AP's Mesolithic sites are in the Nallamala and Kurnool areas. APPSC asks the AP example of a microlith site; Giddalur is the one to remember.

events.title: Neolithic Mehrgarh: earliest farming
events.summary: At Mehrgarh (Baluchistan, about 7000 BCE) people grow wheat and barley and keep sheep and goats — the earliest farming village in the subcontinent.
events.detail: Neolithic people used polished stone tools, made pottery later and lived in mud-brick houses. Other Neolithic sites include Burzahom (Kashmir; pit houses, dogs buried with masters), Chirand (Bihar) and the southern ash-mound sites (Utnur).
causes: Domestication of plants and animals.
outcomes: Farming villages that later grew into the Harappan culture.
events.yearHook: About 7000 BCE at Mehrgarh; about 3000 BCE in the southern Deccan. Farming comes to the south about 4,000 years later.
facts: Neolithic sites: Koldihwa and Mahagara (Belan valley, early rice), Lahuradeva (UP, early rice), Chirand (Bihar), Gufkral and Burzahom (Kashmir), Daojali Hading (Assam).
Southern Neolithic: Brahmagiri, Maski, Piklihal, Sanganakallu, Tekkalakota (Takkalakota), Hallur (Karnataka); Utnur and Palavoy (Andhra–Telangana).
events.before: Mesolithic people (from about 9000 BCE) had begun to tame animals. Slowly they learnt to sow wheat and barley and to live in one place.
events.after: Farming villages grew into towns. In the Indus region they led to the **Early Harappan** phase (about 6000 BCE onwards) and then the great cities (2600 BCE). In the south, herders made the **ash mounds** (about 3000 BCE).
events.today: Mehrgarh is in Baluchistan (Pakistan). Burzahom (Kashmir) shows pit houses dug into the ground.
events.mnemonic: Neolithic firsts: "Mehrgarh = Mother of farming; Burzahom = Buried dogs; Koldihwa = Kept rice".

events.title: Chalcolithic (Copper–Stone) village cultures
events.summary: Chalcolithic (copper–stone) village cultures — Ahar, Kayatha, Malwa and Jorwe — spread across central India and the Deccan.
events.detail: These people used copper along with stone, made painted pottery and grew several crops. Jorwe culture sites include Inamgaon and Daimabad in Maharashtra. Many existed alongside or after the Harappans.
causes: Knowledge of copper smelting.
outcomes: Many villages declined around 1200 BCE with drier conditions.
events.yearHook: From about 3500 BCE, in villages of central India and the Deccan; many lived at the same time as the Harappan cities and after them.
facts: Chalcolithic sites: Ahar and Gilund (Ahar-Banas culture, Rajasthan), Ganeshwar (copper source for Harappans), Navdatoli and Kayatha (MP), Inamgaon–Maharashtra–Chalcolithic, Daimabad, Savalda and Jorwe (Maharashtra), Prabhas and Rangpur (Gujarat), Jodhpura.
Other excavated sites: Atranjikhera (UP, PGW), Bairat (Buddhist remains, Ashokan edict), Chandraketugarh (Bengal), Mangadu–Kerala–Megalithic.
events.before: Neolithic farmers used only stone. When people learnt to smelt **copper**, they used it beside stone tools.
events.after: Most of these villages faded about 1200 BCE as the climate grew drier. In the Deccan and south they were followed by the **iron-using megalith** builders (about 1000 BCE).
events.today: Inamgaon and Daimabad (Maharashtra) are well-known Jorwe sites. Daimabad gave a bronze chariot hoard.
events.mnemonic: Chalcolithic = chalco (copper) + lithic (stone). Cultures "A-K-M-J" from north to south: Ahar, Kayatha, Malwa, Jorwe.

events.title: Early Harappan (Ravi/Hakra) phase begins
events.summary: NCERT dates the Harappan civilisation from 6000 BCE to 1300 BCE; its Early Harappan phase (6000–2600 BCE) is the formative phase (NCERT).
events.detail:
The civilisation is named after Harappa, the first site to be discovered (NCERT). In the early phase farming villages grew in the Indus and Ghaggar–Hakra valleys; NCERT notes that the genetic roots of the Harappans go back to 10,000 BCE.

Early Harappan sites include Kot Diji, Kalibangan (early levels) and Bhirrana. Their pottery, seals and planning slowly developed into the urban culture.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History I, Ch. 1 "Bricks, Beads and Bones"
causes: Growth of farming villages in the Indus region (NCERT).
outcomes: Mature Harappan cities from 2600 BCE (NCERT).
events.yearHook: NCERT's four dates: 6000 → 2600 → 1900 → 1300 BCE = formative → mature cities → decline → late villages.
events.before: Farming villages like **Mehrgarh** (about 7000 BCE) spread along the Indus and the Ghaggar-Hakra rivers.
events.after: By about 2600 BCE these villages had grown into planned cities: the **Mature Harappan** age (next event).
events.today: Bhirrana (Haryana) and Kot Diji (Sindh) show the early levels below the later cities.

events.title: Mature Harappan: planned cities
events.summary: Mature Harappan cities (2600–1900 BCE) have planned streets, covered drains, baked-brick houses, a citadel and a lower town, seals and an undeciphered script (NCERT).
events.detail:
Mohenjodaro had a citadel with the Great Bath and a warehouse, and a lower town with houses around courtyards and no windows on the ground floor (NCERT). Bricks were in a standard ratio of 1:2:4. Lothal had a dockyard and bead-making workshops; Dholavira had water reservoirs; Kalibangan had a ploughed field (NCERT).

Discovery (NCERT): Alexander Cunningham reported a Harappan seal in 1875 without realising its age. Daya Ram Sahni found seals at Harappa (1921) and Rakhal Das Banerji at Mohenjodaro (1922). In 1924 John Marshall announced a new civilisation. Mortimer Wheeler took over the ASI in 1944 and introduced stratigraphic digging.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History I, Ch. 1 "Bricks, Beads and Bones"

alsoOn.text: Daya Ram Sahni begins excavations at Harappa (NCERT).
R.D. Banerji finds Harappan seals at Mohenjodaro (NCERT).
John Marshall announces the Indus civilisation (NCERT).
Alexander Cunningham reports a Harappan seal (NCERT).

events.place: Harappa, Mohenjodaro, Lothal, Dholavira, Kalibangan, Rakhigarhi
causes: Growth of trade, crafts and farming surplus (NCERT).
course: Planned cities with drains (NCERT).
Craft centres at Chanhudaro and Lothal (NCERT).
Trade with Oman, Bahrain and Mesopotamia (NCERT).
Seals with animals and the undeciphered script (NCERT).
outcomes: Decline began about 1900 BCE (NCERT).
facts: The Harappan script was written from right to left and is undeciphered (NCERT).
Rakhigarhi (Haryana) is the largest Harappan site in India.
Dholavira is a UNESCO World Heritage Site (2021).
Other sites: Kalibangan–Mature Harappan (Rajasthan), Banawali (Haryana), Alamgirpur (UP, easternmost), Surkotada (Gujarat, horse remains), Sutkagendor (Baluchistan, westernmost).
The Pashupati seal shows a seated figure with animals.
The script was pictographic and sometimes written boustrophedon (alternate directions).
events.yearHook: 2600–1900 BCE: about 700 years of cities. About 1,000 years before the Rig Veda (about 1500 BCE).
events.before: Over 3,000 years farming villages in the Indus and Ghaggar-Hakra valleys grew rich from farming surplus, crafts and trade (Early Harappan, from about 6000 BCE).
events.after: The cities traded as far as **Mesopotamia** (about 2350 BCE). From about **1900 BCE** they declined and people moved to villages (Late Harappan).
events.today: **Dholavira** (Gujarat) is a UNESCO site (2021); **Rakhigarhi** (Haryana) is the largest Harappan site in India; a museum is being built there.
events.mnemonic: Discoverers "S-B 21-22": Sahni (Harappa, 1921), Banerji (Mohenjodaro, 1922); Marshall announced it (1924). Bricks 1:2:4 (thickness : width : length).

examAngle.point: Boundary sites: Sutkagendor (west, Baluchistan), Alamgirpur (east, UP), Manda (north, J&K), Daimabad (south, Maharashtra).
examAngle.context: APPSC likes "which is NOT a Harappan site": traps are later sites such as Sohgaura (Mauryan copper plate) or Burzahom (Neolithic). Learn the four corners and test any odd name against them.

events.title: Late Harappan: de-urbanisation
events.summary: From about 1900 BCE the Harappan cities decline; by 1800 BCE most sites in Cholistan are abandoned, and the Late Harappan phase lasts to 1300 BCE (NCERT).
events.detail: Seals, weights, special beads and writing disappeared, and people moved to new settlements in Gujarat, Haryana and western UP (NCERT). Explanations include climate change, deforestation, floods, shifting or drying of rivers (such as the Ghaggar–Hakra) and overuse of the land (NCERT). Wheeler's idea of an "Aryan invasion" massacre at Mohenjodaro was disproved by G.F. Dales in 1964 (NCERT).
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History I, Ch. 1 "Bricks, Beads and Bones"
causes: Climate change, floods, drying rivers, overuse of land (NCERT).
outcomes: Rural Late Harappan cultures (1900–1300 BCE) (NCERT).
facts: The "Mythical Massacre at Mohenjodaro" (G.F. Dales, 1964) rejected the invasion theory (NCERT).
Late Harappan cultures were mainly Chalcolithic (stone and copper tools), without metal objects needing complicated casting, and people lived in villages (APPSC Group-1 key).
At Bhagwanpura (Haryana) late Harappan and Painted Grey Ware levels overlap; burnt bricks were found there.
events.yearHook: From about 1900 BCE; the Late Harappan villages last to about 1300 BCE. The Rig Veda is composed from about 1500 BCE.
events.before: For about 700 years (2600–1900 BCE) the cities had flourished.
events.after: People moved east to Haryana, western UP and Gujarat and lived in villages. The **Vedic** people's culture (from about 1500 BCE) grew in the same north-west.
events.today: The debate on why the cities fell (climate, rivers, trade) is still alive; NCERT presents several causes, not one.
events.mnemonic: Causes of decline "CFDO": Climate change, Floods, Drying rivers (Ghaggar-Hakra), Overuse of land. The "Aryan invasion" idea has been rejected.

examAngle.point: Late Harappan cultures were mainly Chalcolithic (stone and copper tools), without metal objects that needed complex casting, and people lived in villages.
examAngle.context: "Late" here means after the cities: writing, seals and special beads disappeared. So any option saying the Late Harappans used complex bronze casting or lived in planned cities is wrong.

events.title: Rig Veda composition begins
events.summary: The Rigveda — 1,028 hymns to gods such as Agni, Indra and Soma — is compiled between about 1500 and 1000 BCE (NCERT).
events.detail:
Early Vedic people were pastoral; wealth was counted in cattle. The tribe (jana) was led by the rajan with the help of the sabha and samiti. The Rigveda is divided into ten mandalas; the Gayatri mantra (to Savitri) is in the third mandala and the Purusha Sukta (four varnas) in the tenth.

NCERT notes that the Rigveda mentions Rudra, a name later used for Shiva. The Battle of Ten Kings (Dasharajna) was fought on the Parushni (Ravi).
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History I, Ch. 4 "Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings"
causes: Settlement in the Sapta Sindhu region.
outcomes: Later Vedic texts (1000–500 BCE) followed (NCERT).
facts: The Rigveda was compiled between c. 1500 and 1000 BCE (NCERT).
Sabha and samiti were assemblies.
Women such as Apala, Ghosha and Lopamudra composed hymns.
Rigvedic rivers: Sindhu (Indus), Vitasta=Jhelum, Asikni=Chenab, Parushni=Ravi, Vipas=Beas, Sutudri=Sutlej, Sarasvati and Drishadvati.
Dasarajna (Battle of Ten Kings): King Sudas of the Bharatas won on the Parushni.
Gods: Indra, Agni, Soma, Varuna (moral order, rita), Maruts (storm gods).
Yajnas (sacrifices) were the main ritual; cattle, not land, was the chief wealth.

Rigvedic gods: Dyaus (sky father, like Jupiter/Zeus), Indra (war, rain), Agni (carried offerings to the gods), Varuna, Soma; cattle (including cow) sacrifice was part of worship. Prithvi was earth, not the mother of all gods (APPSC Group-1 key).

The Boghazkoi inscription (c. 1400 BCE, Anatolia/Turkey) — a treaty between Hittite and Mitanni kings — names the Vedic gods Indra, Varuna, Mitra and the Nasatyas; Mansehra and Shahbazgarhi are Ashokan rock-edict sites in Kharoshthi; Junagarh has Ashoka's edicts and Rudradaman's Sanskrit inscription (APPSC Group-II 2023 key).
events.yearHook: About 1500 BCE: 400 years after the Harappan cities begin to decline (1900 BCE). Early Vedic about 1500–1000 BCE.
events.before: The Harappan cities had faded (from 1900 BCE). People speaking Indo-Aryan languages came through the north-west passes, with horses and chariots, and settled in the land of seven rivers (**Sapta Sindhu**, the Punjab).
events.after: From about 1000 BCE the Vedic people moved east into the Ganga valley, used **iron** and built bigger kingdoms: the **Later Vedic** age (next event).
events.today: The Rig Veda is on UNESCO's **Memory of the World** register (2007). The **Gayatri mantra** (Rig Veda, 3rd mandala, to Savitri) is still chanted daily.
events.mnemonic: Rig Veda numbers "10-1028-250": 10 mandalas (books), 1,028 hymns, about 250 hymns to Indra. Mandalas 2–7 are the oldest (the "family books"); the Purusha Sukta is in the 10th.

examAngle.point: Rigvedic gods: Dyaus (sky father, like Zeus), Indra (war and rain), Agni (fire, carries offerings), Varuna (cosmic order, rita), Soma. Prithvi was the earth, not the mother of all gods.
examAngle.context: Indra has the most hymns (about 250), Agni next (about 200). Cattle, even the cow, were part of sacrifice then. APPSC traps on "Prithvi as mother of all gods".

examAngle.point: The Boghazkoi inscription (about 1400 BCE, Turkey) names the Vedic gods Indra, Varuna, Mitra and the Nasatyas.
examAngle.context: It is a treaty between the Hittite and Mitanni kings. It proves that Indo-Aryan gods were known in West Asia, which supports the idea that the Aryans came from outside India. Mansehra and Shahbazgarhi are Ashokan edict sites; Junagadh has Rudradaman's inscription — all traps in the same question.

events.title: Later Vedic Age: iron & eastward move
events.summary: In the Later Vedic age (about 1000–500 BCE) people settle in the Ganga valley, use iron, form kingdoms (rashtra) and compose the Samaveda, Yajurveda, Atharvaveda, Brahmanas and Upanishads (NCERT).
events.detail: Kings performed big sacrifices such as the rajasuya and ashvamedha (NCERT). Painted Grey Ware pottery and iron tools are found. The varna order became rigid. The Upanishads (c. 800–500 BCE) asked questions about the self (atman) and the universal reality (brahman) (NCERT).
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History I, Ch. 4 "Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings"
causes: Movement east into the Ganga valley; use of iron.
outcomes: Rise of janapadas and mahajanapadas (NCERT).
facts: Some sacrifices were performed by heads of households, others by kings (NCERT).
"Satyameva Jayate" comes from the Mundaka Upanishad.
Prajapati became the supreme god; Varuna declined; Rudra and Vishnu rose.
Ratnins: royal officials such as the Bhagadugha (tax collector), Sangrahitri (treasurer), Suta (charioteer) and Kshattri (chamberlain).
Iron was called Krishna Ayas (Shyama Ayas); copper Lohita Ayas.
Painted Grey Ware (PGW) is the pottery of the age.
Gotra (clan exogamy) and the four ashramas appeared; kings called themselves Ekrat and Chakravartin.
Aranyakas (forest texts) came between the Brahmanas and Upanishads.
Pottery of the Later Vedic people: Black and Red Ware, Black Slipped Ware, Painted Grey Ware and Red Ware; NBPW is later (mahajanapada age) (APPSC Group-1 key).

Six schools of philosophy: Sankhya (Kapila) — the world formed by the blending of prakriti (nature) and purusha; Vaisheshika (Kanada) — atoms are the basis of the world; Nyaya (Gautama, logic); Yoga (Patanjali); Mimamsa (Jaimini); Vedanta (Badarayana).
Heterodox schools: Lokayata/Charvaka — materialism; Ajivika (Makkhali Gosala) — predetermined fate (niyati) (APPSC Group-1 key).
events.yearHook: About 1000–600 BCE: after the Rig Veda, before the Mahajanapadas (600 BCE) and the Buddha (563).
events.before: The Early Vedic people of the Punjab (from about 1500 BCE) were cattle-herding tribes with assemblies (sabha, samiti).
events.after: Bigger farming kingdoms grew into the **16 Mahajanapadas** (about 600 BCE). The Upanishads' questions about the soul and rebirth prepared the ground for **Jainism and Buddhism**.
events.today: The Painted Grey Ware sites (Hastinapur, Atranjikhera) of the Ganga-Yamuna doab are linked with this age.
events.mnemonic: Later Vedic texts "S-Y-A + B-A-U": Sama, Yajur, Atharva Vedas; then Brahmanas, Aranyakas, Upanishads (in that order, ritual → forest → philosophy).

examAngle.point: Later Vedic pottery: Black and Red Ware, Black Slipped Ware, Painted Grey Ware and Red Ware; Northern Black Polished Ware (NBPW) is LATER, of the Mahajanapada age.
examAngle.context: Pottery is a clock for archaeologists: PGW = Later Vedic (about 1000–600 BCE); NBPW = the age of cities and coins (from about 600 BCE).

examAngle.point: Heterodox schools: Lokayata or Charvaka taught materialism; the Ajivikas (Makkhali Gosala) taught fixed fate (niyati).
examAngle.context: "Heterodox" (nastika) schools reject the Vedas. Besides Charvaka and Ajivika, Jainism and Buddhism are the big ones. Gosala travelled with Mahavira for six years before founding the Ajivikas.

events.title: Sixteen Mahajanapadas emerge
events.summary: By the sixth century BCE there are sixteen mahajanapadas (great states) in Buddhist and Jaina texts, among them Magadha, Kosala, Vajji, Kuru, Panchala, Gandhara, Avanti and Assaka (NCERT).
events.detail:
Most were ruled by kings; some, such as the Vajji and the Shakyas, were ganas or sanghas ruled by assemblies (NCERT). Each had a fortified capital. Rulers collected taxes and tribute from farmers, traders and craftsmen and kept armies (NCERT).

Assaka (Ashmaka), on the Godavari, was the only mahajanapada in south India; its capital was Potana or Podana (Bodhan, Telangana). Punch-marked coins and urbanisation in the Ganga valley also appear now (NCERT).
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History I, Ch. 2 "Kings, Farmers and Towns"
causes: Iron tools, paddy transplantation and surplus (NCERT).
outcomes: Magadha became the most powerful (NCERT).
facts: Paddy transplantation and punch-marked coins c. 600–500 BCE (NCERT).
Lists in the Anguttara Nikaya (Buddhist) and the Bhagavati Sutra (Jaina).

Capitals: Magadha–Rajagriha (Girivraja), Kosala–Shravasti, Vatsa–Kausambi, Avanti–Ujjayini and Mahishmati, Kuru–Indraprastha (and Hastinapur), Panchala–Ahichhatra and Kampilya, Kashi–Varanasi (Rajghat), Anga–Champa, Chedi–Suktimati, Surasena–Mathura, Matsya–Viratnagar (Bairat), Assaka (Asmaka)–Potali/Potana, Gandhara–Taxila, Kamboja–Rajapura (Poonch region), Malla–Kushinara (Kusinagara) and Pava, Vajji (Vriji)–Vaishali.
Ganas: the Shakyas (Kapilavastu), Koliyas, Mallas and Lichchhavis were ruled by assemblies.
Officials: Mahamatras (high officers), Senanayaka (commander), Gramabhojaka/Gramini (village headman).
Northern Black Polished Ware (NBPW) is the pottery of the mahajanapada age.
Mahajanapadas formed by the amalgamation of a large number of rural settlements (janapadas).
events.yearHook: About 600 BCE: the century of the Buddha (563) and Mahavira (599).
events.before: Later Vedic tribes (1000–600 BCE) settled down; the tribe's land (**janapada**) grew into a big state (**mahajanapada**). Iron ploughs gave surplus grain; towns, trade and **punch-marked coins** appeared (the "second urbanisation").
events.after: The four big ones fought for 200 years. **Magadha** won under Bimbisara (544 BCE), the Shishunagas and the Nandas, and became the first empire.
events.today: The list of 16 comes from the Buddhist **Anguttara Nikaya** (and the Jain Bhagavati Sutra gives a different list). Assaka on the Godavari is the Andhra-Telangana link.
events.mnemonic: Four big ones fought for power: "MAKV" = Magadha, Avanti, Kosala, Vatsa. Only Assaka (Asmaka) lay south of the Vindhyas, on the Godavari.

events.title: Birth of Mahavira (24th Tirthankara)
events.summary: Vardhamana Mahavira, the 24th tirthankara of the Jainas, is born at Kundagrama near Vaishali (traditionally 599 BCE).
events.detail:
He left home at 30, practised hard penance for 12 years and attained kevala jnana. He taught that the entire world is animated — even stones, rocks and water have life — and that non-injury (ahimsa) to all living beings is central (NCERT). He preached in Prakrit.

Jainism was later split into Digambaras (sky-clad) and Shvetambaras (white-clad). Jaina texts were compiled at Valabhi (Gujarat).
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History I, Ch. 4 "Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings"
causes: Questioning of Vedic sacrifices and the varna order (NCERT).
outcomes: Jainism spread to Karnataka, Gujarat and Rajasthan (NCERT).
events.yearHook: 599 BCE in the Jain count (540 BCE in another). The Buddha is born about 563 BCE: about 36 years later.
events.before: In the 6th century BCE, the age of the **16 Mahajanapadas**, there was unrest about religion. Vedic sacrifices were costly; Brahmana priests claimed the top rank. Kshatriyas and traders (Vaishyas) wanted a simpler, fairer path. Many teachers rose to offer one: Mahavira, the Buddha, Makkhali Gosala and others.
events.after: At 30 Mahavira left home; at 42 he attained **Kaivalya** (about 557 BCE) and began to teach (next event).
events.today: Kundagrama (Kundalpur) near **Vaishali** in Bihar is honoured as his birthplace. His birthday is **Mahavir Jayanti**.
events.mnemonic: Mahavira's family "S-T-Y": Siddhartha (father), Trishala (mother), Yashoda (wife). Do not mix Yashoda with the Buddha's wife Yashodhara.

examAngle.point: Mahavira's father Siddhartha led the Jnatrika clan; his mother Trishala was a Lichchhavi princess, sister of Chetaka, the chief of Vaishali.
examAngle.context: Mahavira was a Kshatriya prince of the Vajji (Vrijji) confederacy, one of the republics (ganas) of the age. Note the trap: Siddhartha is also the Buddha's own name; the Buddha's father was Suddhodana.

events.title: Birth of Gautama Buddha at Lumbini
events.summary: Siddhartha Gautama, the future Buddha, is born at Lumbini to the Shakya chief Suddhodana (traditionally 563 BCE).
events.detail: He belonged to a small gana, the Shakyas. Shaken by the sight of an old man, a sick man and a corpse, and then a calm ascetic, he left home to seek the truth (NCERT). Lumbini is marked by Ashoka's pillar, which says the village was exempted from tax.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History I, Ch. 4 "Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings"
causes: Search for an end to suffering (NCERT).
outcomes: Enlightenment at Bodh Gaya (c. 528 BCE).
events.yearHook: 563 BCE. Then add 35 to reach enlightenment (528) and 80 to reach his death (483): "563 → 528 → 483".
facts: Born at Lumbini near Kapilavastu to Suddhodana and Mahamaya of the Sakya clan — hence "Sakyamuni" (sage of the Sakyas).
Piprahwa (near Kapilavastu) yielded a relic casket; the Piprahwa relics returned to India in 2025.
events.before: In the 6th century BCE the **16 Mahajanapadas** were growing into big kingdoms. Cities, trade and coins were spreading, and so was unrest with costly Vedic sacrifices and the power of priests. Many wandering teachers (**shramanas**) offered new paths; Mahavira was one of them, about 36 years older than the Buddha.
events.after: At 29 he left home (the **Great Renunciation**, mahabhinishkramana). After six years of seeking he was enlightened at Bodh Gaya at 35 (528 BCE, next event).
events.today: **Lumbini** (now in Nepal) is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Ashoka's Rummindei pillar there says he cut the village's tax to one-eighth. **Kapilavastu** is linked with Piprahwa (UP) and Tilaurakot (Nepal).
events.mnemonic: Four sights "OSDA": an Old man, a Sick man, a Dead body, an Ascetic. The fourth one showed him a way out.

events.title: Bimbisara founds Magadha ascendancy (Haryanka)
events.summary: Bimbisara of the Haryanka dynasty becomes king of Magadha (c. 544 BCE) and makes it powerful through marriage alliances and the conquest of Anga.
events.detail:
NCERT explains Magadha's rise: fertile land, iron mines, elephants in the forests, the Ganga and its tributaries for transport, and ambitious kings such as Bimbisara, Ajatashatru and Mahapadma Nanda. Rajagriha was the first capital; later it moved to Pataliputra.

Bimbisara married princesses of Kosala, Vaishali and Madra, and received Kashi as dowry. His son Ajatashatru killed him and fought Kosala and the Vajjis; Udayin moved the capital to Pataliputra.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History I, Ch. 2 "Kings, Farmers and Towns"
causes: Fertile land, iron, elephants, rivers (NCERT).
outcomes: Magadha became the leading mahajanapada (NCERT).
facts: Rajagriha (Rajgir) was a fortified settlement among hills (NCERT).
Rivals: Chanda Pradyota of Avanti, Prasenajit of Kosala, Chetaka of the Lichchhavis (Ajatashatru's maternal grandfather).
Magadha lay between the Ganga, Son and Gandak rivers; Girivraja was the old name of Rajagriha.

alsoOn.text: Ajatashatru kills Bimbisara and becomes king of Magadha.

events.yearHook: 544 BCE: the Buddha (born 563) is about 19; Mahavira (599) is about 55. Both were his contemporaries.

participants.role: Later king who built on Magadha's rise (NCERT).

events.before: Of the 16 Mahajanapadas (about 600 BCE), four were strongest. Magadha had iron, elephants, fertile land and rivers on three sides.
events.after: His son **Ajatashatru** (about 492 BCE) took the throne and pushed the empire wider (next event).
events.today: Rajgir (Rajagriha) in Bihar has Bimbisara's jail and the cyclopean wall.

events.title: Buddha's enlightenment at Bodh Gaya
events.summary: Siddhartha attains enlightenment under a peepal tree at Bodh Gaya (c. 528 BCE) and gives his first sermon at Sarnath (NCERT).
events.detail: After trying severe penance he chose the Middle Path. He taught that the world is transient and constantly changing, that suffering comes from desire, and that it ends by following the Eightfold Path (NCERT). He spoke in Pali, the language of ordinary people. He formed the sangha of monks; later nuns were admitted at the request of Ananda (NCERT).
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History I, Ch. 4 "Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings"
causes: Search for the end of suffering (NCERT).
outcomes: Sangha founded; Buddhism spread (NCERT).
facts: First sermon: Dhammachakkapavattana ("turning of the wheel of dhamma") at Sarnath.
Mahapajapati Gotami was the first woman ordained (NCERT).
Enlightened under a pipal tree (Bodhi tree) at Bodh Gaya.

Four Noble Truths: dukkha (suffering), samudaya (cause = trishna/tanha, desire), nirodha (cessation = nirvana/nibbana, "extinction of the flame of desire"), magga (the Ashtangika Marga, Eightfold Path).
Middle Path: avoid extreme luxury and extreme austerity.
Buddhism taught anatman (no permanent self), karma over birth, and accepted no creator God.
Mahabodhi temple stands at Bodh Gaya (UNESCO).
events.before: After leaving home he studied under two teachers (**Alara Kalama** and **Udraka Ramaputra**) and then tried hard fasting for six years. It nearly killed him. He gave it up and chose the **Middle Path** between luxury and starving.
events.after: Weeks later he gave his **first sermon** to five old companions in the **deer park at Sarnath** (near Varanasi): the "turning of the wheel of dhamma" (dhammachakkapavattana). He founded the **sangha** (order of monks; nuns joined later at Ananda's request) and taught for 45 years until his death at Kushinagar (483 BCE).
events.today: The **Mahabodhi temple** at Bodh Gaya is a UNESCO site. The Sarnath lion capital of Ashoka is India's **national emblem**, and the wheel (chakra) is on the **national flag**.
events.mnemonic: Four Noble Truths "S-C-C-P": Suffering, its Cause (desire), its Cessation (nirvana), the Path (eightfold). Eightfold path starts with "Right View" and ends with "Right Concentration".

events.title: Mahaparinirvana of the Buddha; First Council
events.summary: The Buddha dies at Kusinagara at the age of 80 (c. 483 BCE) — his mahaparinibbana (NCERT).
events.detail: His relics were divided and stupas built over them; NCERT explains that Ashoka later redistributed them and built stupas everywhere. Sanchi, Bharhut and Amaravati are famous stupas (NCERT).
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History I, Ch. 4 "Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings"
causes: Old age.
outcomes: First Buddhist Council at Rajagriha.
Stupas built over his relics (NCERT).
events.yearHook: 483 BCE, at the age of 80: 563 − 80 = 483. The First Council meets the same year.

participants.role: Redistributed the relics and built stupas (NCERT).

facts: Died at Kushinagar (Kusinagara) — Mahaparinirvana.
events.before: For 45 years after his enlightenment (528 BCE) the Buddha walked through **Magadha and Kosala**, teaching in **Pali**, the people's language. Kings Bimbisara and Prasenajit and rich merchants such as Anathapindika supported him.
events.after: His relics were shared among eight groups, who built stupas over them. The **First Council** met at Rajagriha the same year to collect his teachings (next event). Two centuries later **Ashoka** opened the relic stupas and built many more.
events.today: Kushinagar (Uttar Pradesh) has the Mahaparinirvana temple with a reclining Buddha, and an international airport (2021) for Buddhist pilgrims.
events.mnemonic: Four holy places of his life "L-B-S-K": Lumbini (birth), Bodh Gaya (enlightenment), Sarnath (first sermon), Kushinagar (death).

events.title: Second Buddhist Council at Vaishali
events.summary: The Second Buddhist Council meets at Vaishali (c. 383 BCE) under King Kalashoka; the sangha splits into Sthaviravadins and Mahasanghikas.
events.detail: The dispute was over ten points of monastic discipline, such as monks accepting gold and silver. It was presided over by Sabakami. It marked the first split in Buddhism.
causes: Disputes over monastic rules.
outcomes: Split into Sthaviravada and Mahasanghika.
events.yearHook: 383 BCE: 100 years after the Buddha's death (483 − 100).
facts: Held under Kalasoka (Kakavarna), the Shishunaga king.
events.before: The First Council (483 BCE) had fixed the rules, but some monks at Vaishali began to relax them, for example by taking gold and silver.
events.after: The split into **Sthaviravadins** (the elders, strict) and **Mahasanghikas** (the "great community", more open) began. The Mahasanghikas later grew strong in **Andhra** and fed into Mahayana.
events.today: Vaishali (Bihar) has an Ashokan lion pillar and the relic stupa of the Lichchhavis.

events.title: Mahapadma Nanda founds the Nanda dynasty
events.summary: Mahapadma Nanda overthrows the Shishunagas and founds the Nanda dynasty of Magadha (c. 345 BCE), with a huge army and treasury.
events.detail: The Nandas were said to be of low birth; Mahapadma was called "ekarat" (sole ruler). They conquered Kalinga. Greek writers say the last Nanda, Dhana Nanda, had 20,000 cavalry, 200,000 infantry, 2,000 chariots and 3,000 elephants, which made Alexander's soldiers unwilling to advance. Chandragupta Maurya and Chanakya overthrew him.
causes: Weak Shishunaga rule.
outcomes: Overthrown by Chandragupta Maurya (c. 321 BCE).
events.yearHook: About 345 BCE; the Nandas end in 321 BCE when Chandragupta Maurya takes Pataliputra.
events.before: The Shishunagas (from about 413 BCE) had removed Avanti, Magadha's last big rival.
events.after: Alexander reached the Beas (326 BCE) but turned back, partly for fear of the Nanda army. **Dhana Nanda**, the last king, was unpopular for heavy taxes; **Chandragupta Maurya** and **Chanakya** overthrew him (321 BCE).
events.today: Kharavela's Hathigumpha inscription (Odisha) says a Nanda king had dug a canal in Kalinga — proof that the Nandas ruled there.
events.mnemonic: Nanda = "first non-Kshatriya empire". Mahapadma = "Sarvakshatrantaka", the destroyer of all Kshatriyas.

events.title: Alexander's invasion; Battle of Hydaspes
events.summary: Alexander of Macedon invades the north-west (327–325 BCE) (NCERT) and defeats Porus at the Hydaspes (Jhelum) in 326 BCE; his army refuses to go beyond the Beas.
events.detail: Ambhi, king of Taxila, submitted and helped Alexander. Porus fought with elephants but lost because of the cavalry and the wet ground. Impressed, Alexander restored him as ruler. At the Beas his tired soldiers, who had heard of the Nandas' army, refused to go on. Alexander left via the Indus and died at Babylon in 323 BCE.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History I, Ch. 2 "Kings, Farmers and Towns"; Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)
causes: Alexander's campaign to conquer the Persian empire and beyond.
course: 327 BCE: Alexander crosses the Hindu Kush.
Ambhi of Taxila submits.
326 BCE: battle of the Hydaspes.
Army refuses to cross the Beas.
325 BCE: retreat.
losses: Porus's army heavily defeated.
outcomes: Greek satrapies in the north-west, soon taken by Chandragupta.
Opened land and sea routes between India and the West.

pairs.left: Admiral who led the fleet back

events.yearHook: 326 BCE; Chandragupta Maurya rises five years later (321 BCE).

participants.role: Fought and lost; restored as ruler.
His big army discouraged Alexander's soldiers.

facts: Alexander (born 356 BCE) became king in 336 BCE; won at Chaeronea (338 BCE, with his father) and Gaugamela (Arbela, 331 BCE) against Darius III.
His teacher was Aristotle.
He founded Alexandria Bucephala (after his horse) and Nicaea on the Jhelum; Abhisara's king sided with Porus.
Nearchus led the fleet home; histories by Arrian, Curtius, Diodorus and Plutarch.
events.before: Persian rule in the north-west (from about 518 BCE) had weakened. Alexander of Macedonia, son of **Philip II**, had beaten Persia's Darius III (331 BCE) and marched to India. **Ambhi** of Taxila welcomed him.
events.after: Porus fought bravely and was treated as a king. Alexander went on to the **Beas**, where his army refused to go further (next event).
events.today: The battle site is on the Jhelum river in Pakistani Punjab.
events.mnemonic: At Hydaspes, ask "Ambhi helped, Porus fought": Ambhi of Taxila joined Alexander; Porus of the Paurava kingdom fought him.

events.title: Chandragupta Maurya founds the Mauryan Empire
events.summary: Chandragupta Maurya, helped by Chanakya, overthrows the Nandas and founds the Mauryan empire (c. 321 BCE) (NCERT).
events.detail:
Chandragupta's empire extended as far north-west as Afghanistan and Baluchistan (NCERT). Sources for the Mauryas include the Arthashastra (traditionally Chanakya's), the account of Megasthenes, later Buddhist and Jaina texts, the Sanskrit play Mudrarakshasa, and Ashoka's inscriptions (NCERT).

Pataliputra was the capital, with provincial centres at Taxila, Ujjayini, Tosali and Suvarnagiri (NCERT). A committee of 30 members in six subcommittees managed the army (NCERT, from Megasthenes).
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History I, Ch. 2 "Kings, Farmers and Towns"
causes: Unpopularity of the Nandas.
Power vacuum after Alexander.
outcomes: First empire covering most of the subcontinent (NCERT).
facts: Mudrarakshasa by Vishakhadatta tells of Chanakya's plots against the Nandas.
Four provincial centres: Taxila, Ujjayini, Tosali, Suvarnagiri (NCERT).
Officials: Rajukas (rural administration), Yuktas (revenue clerks), Pradeshikas (district heads), Samaharta (revenue), Sannidhata (treasury).
Arthashastra: Saptanga theory (seven limbs of the state), Mantriparishad (council).
The Chandragupta–Seleucus war ended in a treaty (c. 305 BCE).
The Sohgaura copper plate and Mahasthan inscription record Mauryan famine relief (storehouses).
Kautilya lists 18 tirthas (high officers); Dandapala was the officer of the army department (APPSC Group-1 key).

Arthashastra superintendents (adhyakshas): Pautavadhyaksha — weights and measures; Sulkadhyaksha — tolls and customs; Panyadhyaksha — trade/commerce; Sitadhyaksha — crown lands; Akaradhyaksha — mines; Lakshanadhyaksha — mint; Sunadhyaksha — slaughter-houses; Navadhyaksha — ships; Ganikadhyaksha — courtesans (APPSC Group-II 2023 key).
Sohgaura (Gorakhpur, UP) is a Mauryan copper-plate inscription site about famine-relief granaries — not a Harappan site (unlike Sutkagendor, Surkotada, Rakhigarhi) (APPSC Group-II 2023 key).

participants.role: His inscriptions are a major source (NCERT).

events.title: Chandragupta defeats Seleucus; treaty
events.summary: Chandragupta Maurya defeats Seleucus Nicator (c. 305 BCE); by treaty Seleucus cedes the north-western provinces for 500 war elephants and sends Megasthenes as ambassador.
events.detail: Seleucus, Alexander's general, tried to recover the Indian provinces. The war ended with a treaty and a marriage alliance. Megasthenes lived at Pataliputra and wrote the Indica, known from later quotations (NCERT).
causes: Seleucus's attempt to regain Alexander's Indian conquests.

treaties.name: Treaty of Chandragupta and Seleucus
terms: Seleucus ceded Arachosia (Kandahar), Gedrosia (Baluchistan) and Paropamisadae (Kabul) and probably Aria (Herat).
Chandragupta gave 500 war elephants.
A marriage alliance (epigamia).
Megasthenes sent as ambassador.

gains: Afghanistan and Baluchistan for the Mauryas.
outcomes: Friendly Mauryan–Greek relations; Greek envoys at Pataliputra.
events.yearHook: c. 305 BCE — 16 years after the Mauryas began.
facts: Other Greek writers: Ktesias (Persia), Deimachus (Bindusara's court), Dionysius (Ptolemy II's envoy).
Pliny the Elder (Naturalis Historia) complained of Roman gold flowing to India; Ptolemy wrote the Geographia; the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea described Indian ports.
The Silk Route linked China, Central Asia and India.

events.title: Jain councils & split (Digambara/Svetambara)
events.summary: During a long famine Bhadrabahu leads Jaina monks to Karnataka with Chandragupta Maurya; the First Jaina Council at Pataliputra under Sthulabhadra compiles the texts, and the split into Digambaras and Shvetambaras follows.
events.detail: Monks who stayed in Magadha under Sthulabhadra began wearing white (Shvetambaras); those who returned from the south kept the rule of nudity (Digambaras). The Second Jaina Council at Valabhi (5th century CE, under Devardhi Kshamashramana) wrote down the 12 Angas. Chandragupta died at Shravanabelagola.
causes: A 12-year famine in Magadha.
outcomes: Digambara–Shvetambara split.
Jainism spread in Karnataka.
events.yearHook: About 300 BCE, in Chandragupta Maurya's last years (he gives up the throne about 297 BCE).
events.before: A 12-year famine struck Magadha. **Bhadrabahu** led a group of monks south to Karnataka; **Chandragupta Maurya** went with him. **Sthulabhadra** stayed back in Magadha.
events.after: The two groups grew apart. Those who went south kept to nudity and became the **Digambaras**; those who stayed wore white and became the **Svetambaras**. Each later split into sub-sects. The canon was finally written down at **Vallabhi** (512 CE).
events.today: Digambara and Svetambara temples look different: Digambara images are nude with eyes cast down; Svetambara images are adorned, with eyes open.
events.mnemonic: "Digambara = Directions as clothes (sky-clad); Svetambara = Snow-white clad". "Bhadrabahu went south, Sthulabhadra stayed".

events.title: Sangam Age: Tamil academies at Madurai
events.summary: The Sangam age of Tamil literature begins; the Cholas, Cheras and Pandyas rule in the far south (NCERT notes them in c. 200–100 BCE).
events.detail: Tradition speaks of three Sangams (assemblies of poets) at Madurai under Pandya patronage. Sangam poems are divided into akam (love) and puram (war and public life). The Tolkappiyam is a Tamil grammar; the epics Silappadikaram (Ilango Adigal) and Manimekalai (Sittalai Sattanar) come later. Ashoka's inscriptions mention the Cholas, Pandyas, Keralaputras and Satiyaputras.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History I, Ch. 2 "Kings, Farmers and Towns"; Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)
causes: Growth of chiefdoms and trade in the far south.
outcomes: Roman trade at Arikamedu and Muziris.

participants.role: His edicts name the southern kingdoms.

facts: Sangam literature: Tolkappiyam (by Tolkappiyar), Ettuthokai (eight anthologies), Pattuppattu (ten idylls), Pathinenkilkanakku (eighteen minor works, including the Tirukkural).
The three crowned kings (Muvendar): Cheras (capital Vanji, port Muziris/Tondi, emblem bow), Cholas (Uraiyur, Puhar, tiger), Pandyas (Madurai, port Korkai, carp/fish).
Kings: Udiyanjeral and Imayavaramban Nedum Cheralathan (Chera); Cheran Senguttuvan built a temple to Kannagi; Nedunjeliyan (Pandya, Talaiyalanganam).
Gajabahu synchronism: Gajabahu of Sri Lanka attended Senguttuvan's Kannagi festival, used to date the Sangam age (c.300 BCE–300 CE).
Sangam poems divide land into five tinai (landscapes); irai = tax; iravu = gift-asking.
Keeladi (near Madurai) excavations show an urban Sangam settlement; the Chola Elara ruled in Sri Lanka.
In Sangam society the Vellalars were rich peasants who formed the fourth caste; the Arasar were the ruling class; Kadaisiyar were the lowest labourers (APPSC Group-1 key).

events.title: Ashoka ascends the Mauryan throne
events.summary: Ashoka becomes Mauryan emperor (c. 272/268 BCE) (NCERT) after a struggle with his brothers; he is the first ruler to inscribe his messages on stone (NCERT).
events.detail: Ashoka had been viceroy at Ujjain and Taxila. Buddhist texts say he fought his brothers for the throne and was crowned four years later. His inscriptions call him "Devanampiya Piyadassi"; the name Ashoka appears in only a few, such as Maski (Karnataka) and Gujarra (MP). James Prinsep deciphered his Brahmi script in 1838 (NCERT).
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History I, Ch. 2 "Kings, Farmers and Towns"
causes: Death of Bindusara.
outcomes: Kalinga war (c. 261 BCE) (NCERT).
facts: Most Ashokan inscriptions are in Prakrit and Brahmi; in the north-west Kharosthi; in Afghanistan Aramaic and Greek (NCERT).
Maski inscription names "Ashoka".
He is called Devanampiya Piyadasi; his name appears at Maski, Gujarra, Nettur and Udegolam.
Major rock edicts: Dhauli–Odisha, Jaugada (Odisha), Girnar (Gujarat), Kalsi (Uttarakhand), Erragudi–Andhra, Sopara, Shahbazgarhi.
Bindusara "Amitraghata" ("slayer of foes").

alsoOn.text: James Prinsep deciphers Ashokan Brahmi (NCERT).

events.title: Kalinga War; Ashoka embraces Buddhism
events.summary: Ashoka conquers Kalinga (coastal Odisha, c. 261 BCE) (NCERT); the suffering it causes makes him give up war and turn to dhamma, as he says in Rock Edict XIII.
events.detail:
In Rock Edict XIII Ashoka says that 150,000 people were deported, 100,000 killed and many more died. He felt deep remorse and decided that conquest by dhamma (dhamma-vijaya) was the best conquest (NCERT).

His dhamma was not a religion but a set of moral principles: respect for elders, kindness to slaves and servants, generosity towards brahmanas and shramanas, and respect for other sects (NCERT). He appointed dhamma mahamattas to spread it (NCERT). He renounced bherighosha (the sound of war drums) for dhammaghosha.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History I, Ch. 2 "Kings, Farmers and Towns"
causes: Kalinga controlled the land and sea routes to the south.
losses: 100,000 killed and 150,000 deported (Rock Edict XIII).
gains: Kalinga added to the empire; Tosali a provincial capital (NCERT).
outcomes: Ashoka's policy of dhamma (NCERT).
Missions to Sri Lanka, Central Asia and the Hellenistic kingdoms.
facts: The only war Ashoka fought.
Dhauli and Jaugada edicts (Odisha) contain the Separate Kalinga Edicts.
events.yearHook: c. 261 BCE — about 8 years after his coronation.

participants.role: Sent to Sri Lanka as a missionary.
Sent to Sri Lanka with a Bodhi sapling.

events.title: Ashokan Mauryas reach the Andhra country
events.summary: Ashoka's inscriptions at Amaravati, Erragudi (Kurnool) and Rajula Mandagiri show that the Andhra region was part of the Mauryan empire; his edicts name the Andhras as a people within his realm.
events.detail: Rock Edict XIII lists the Andhras among peoples following his dhamma. Erragudi near Gooty in Kurnool district has a set of major and minor rock edicts. Amaravati has a fragment of a pillar edict. Buddhism spread along the Krishna valley from this time.
events.source: AP SCERT; Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)
causes: Mauryan expansion into the Deccan.
outcomes: Buddhism spread in Andhra; Bhattiprolu and Amaravati stupas later.
events.yearHook: About 260 BCE. Ashoka's Kalinga war was in 261 BCE, and Kalinga (Odisha) borders north Andhra.

participants.role: His edicts are found in Andhra.

events.before: **Chandragupta Maurya** founded the Mauryan empire in 321 BCE. His grandson **Ashoka** fought the **Kalinga war** (261 BCE), right next door to Andhra. Shocked by the killing, he turned to Buddhism and **dhamma**, a code of good conduct he carved on rocks and pillars all over his empire.
events.after: Mauryan rule brought roads, writing (the **Brahmi** script) and Buddhist monks into Andhra. When the Mauryas grew weak after Ashoka died (232 BCE), local chiefs rose. One of them, **Simuka**, started the **Satavahana** dynasty in about 230 BCE. That is the next big event.
events.today: The **Erragudi** (Yerragudi) edicts stand near Gooty, on the Kurnool–Anantapuramu border. **Rajula Mandagiri** is also in Kurnool district. A broken pillar edict was found at **Amaravati**.
events.mnemonic: Ashoka in Andhra: "AER" = Amaravati, Erragudi, Rajula Mandagiri.

examAngle.point: Ashoka's Rock Edict XIII names the Andhras among the peoples of his empire.
examAngle.context: This is the first time the Andhras appear in a royal inscription. Rock Edict XIII is also where Ashoka speaks of his sorrow after Kalinga. So one edict links three things: Kalinga, dhamma and the Andhras. (Earlier still, the Vedic text **Aitareya Brahmana** names the Andhras as a people.)

events.title: Ashokan pillars & Sarnath capital
events.summary: Ashoka sets up polished sandstone pillars with animal capitals and inscriptions; the lion capital of Sarnath becomes India's national emblem.
events.detail: The pillars were made of Chunar sandstone with a mirror-like Mauryan polish. Seven pillar edicts and fourteen major rock edicts carry his dhamma. Famous capitals: four lions (Sarnath), one lion (Lauriya Nandangarh), bull (Rampurva). The Lumbini pillar records his visit and the tax cut.
causes: Ashoka's wish to spread dhamma (NCERT).
outcomes: The Sarnath lion capital adopted as the national emblem (26 January 1950).
facts: The Rummindei (Lumbini) pillar inscription says Ashoka reduced Lumbini's land revenue to one-eighth (atthabhagiya) and exempted it from bali (APPSC Group-II 2023 key).

events.title: Third Buddhist Council under Ashoka
events.summary: The Third Buddhist Council meets at Pataliputra (c. 250 BCE) under Ashoka and Moggaliputta Tissa; the Abhidhamma Pitaka is completed and missionaries are sent abroad.
events.detail: The council expelled dissident monks and compiled the Kathavatthu. Missions went to Sri Lanka (Mahinda and Sanghamitta), Suvarnabhumi (Myanmar/Thailand), Kashmir and Gandhara.
causes: Disputes in the sangha.
outcomes: Abhidhamma Pitaka; Buddhism spread abroad.
events.yearHook: About 250 BCE: about 11 years after the Kalinga war (261 BCE).
facts: Kanganahalli (Karnataka) has an image labelled "Ranyo Ashoka" (King Ashoka).
The council compiled the Kathavatthu and completed the Abhidhamma Pitaka.
events.before: After Kalinga (261 BCE) Ashoka turned to the Buddha's teaching. Many quarrelling groups had entered the sangha for its royal gifts.
events.after: Ashoka sent missionaries abroad: his son **Mahinda** and daughter **Sanghamitta** to **Sri Lanka**, others to Suvarnabhumi (Myanmar/Thailand), Kashmir and Gandhara. About 350 years later the **Fourth Council** in Kashmir saw Mahayana take shape.
events.today: Sri Lanka still honours the sapling of the Bodhi tree that Sanghamitta took there (at Anuradhapura).

events.title: Death of Ashoka; Mauryan decline
events.summary: Ashoka dies (c. 232/231 BCE) (NCERT); the empire weakens under his successors and ends when Pushyamitra Shunga kills the last Maurya, Brihadratha, in about 185 BCE (NCERT).
events.detail: Reasons for the decline include weak successors, division of the empire, the heavy cost of the army and administration, and pressure from the north-west. Some historians blamed Ashoka's policy of non-violence; others reject this.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History I, Ch. 2 "Kings, Farmers and Towns"
causes: Weak successors; financial strain.
outcomes: Shunga rule from c. 185 BCE (NCERT).

events.title: Simuka founds the Satavahana dynasty
events.summary: Simuka founds the Satavahana dynasty of the Deccan (c. 230 BCE); called "Andhras" in the Puranas, it rules from Pratishthana (Paithan) and later Dhanyakataka (Amaravati) (NCERT notes Satavahanas in the Deccan c. 200–100 BCE).
events.detail:
The Satavahanas rose after the Mauryan decline. Satakarni I performed the ashvamedha (Naneghat inscription of queen Naganika). Gautamiputra Satakarni (c. 106–130 CE) defeated the Shakas; his mother's Nasik inscription praises him (NCERT). Vasishthiputra Pulumavi shifted east to Andhra.

They issued lead and potin coins and ship-marked coins, gave the earliest land grants to brahmanas and Buddhist monks (NCERT), and used Prakrit. Their kings used metronymics such as Gautamiputra (son of Gautami) (NCERT). Hala compiled the Gathasaptashati.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History I, Ch. 2 "Kings, Farmers and Towns"; Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
causes: Mauryan decline in the Deccan.
outcomes: Ruled the Deccan for about 450 years; succeeded in Andhra by the Ikshvakus.
facts: Karle Chaitya (Maharashtra) is the largest rock-cut chaitya of their age.
Satavahana dancers used a foundation cream called Aradalam (APPSC Group-II 2018 key).
events.yearHook: About 230 BCE, just after Ashoka dies (232 BCE). Satavahanas last from about 230 BCE to 225 CE, roughly 450 years.

participants.role: Shifted the kingdom east to Andhra.

events.before: After Ashoka died in 232 BCE, the Mauryan empire broke up. In the Deccan, local chiefs who had served the Mauryas made themselves kings. The **Puranas** (old books of kings) call these new kings "Andhras" or "**Andhra-bhrityas**" (servants of the Andhras).
events.after:
The Satavahanas ruled the Deccan for about 450 years.

1. **Early kings** (Simuka, Kanha, Satakarni I) ruled from the west, around Pratishthana (Paithan, Maharashtra).
2. **Shakas** (the Western Kshatrapas, foreigners from Central Asia) took their western lands in the 1st century CE.
3. **Gautamiputra Satakarni** (about 106 CE) won them back. That is the next Satavahana event.
4. **Later kings** moved east to the Krishna valley, with **Dhanyakataka** (Amaravati) as capital.
5. In about **225 CE** they gave way to the **Ikshvakus** in Andhra.
events.today: **Dharanikota**, near Amaravati, is the old Dhanyakataka. **Paithan** (Pratishthana) in Maharashtra still makes Paithani silk saris. The new AP capital is named **Amaravati** after this Satavahana-age city.
events.mnemonic: Kings in order: "Six Kings Sat; Hala Gave Poems Yearly" = Simuka, Kanha, Satakarni I, Hala, Gautamiputra, Pulumavi, Yajna Sri.

examAngle.point: Satavahana kings took their mother's name: Gautamiputra ("son of Gautami"), Vasishthiputra.
examAngle.context: This is a **metronymic**. It does NOT mean the family followed the mother's line; the throne still passed from father to son. It shows how much royal mothers were honoured. For example, Gautami Balashri wrote the Nasik inscription for her son.

examAngle.point: Queen Naganika (Nayanika) wrote the Naneghat inscription and ruled as regent for her young son.
examAngle.context: After her husband Satakarni I died, she ran the kingdom until her son grew up. The Naneghat inscription (on a mountain pass near Pune) records Satakarni I's Vedic sacrifices, including the **ashvamedha** (horse sacrifice). Naneghat and Nasik are in Maharashtra, so the early Satavahanas were in the west, not yet in Andhra.

examAngle.point: Hala's Gathasaptasati, 700 love poems in Prakrit, is the best source for Satavahana social life.
examAngle.context: Hala was the 17th king (1st century CE). His poems show village life, farming, festivals and love. Do not mix it up with **Gunadhya's Brihatkatha**, written in Paishachi Prakrit, not Sanskrit.

examAngle.point: The earliest land grants known from inscriptions are by the Satavahanas (and the Shakas), about 100–200 CE.
examAngle.context: Kings gave villages, free of tax, to Brahmanas and Buddhist monks. Later dynasties gave many more grants, which created a new class of landlords. NCERT links this to the debate on the "beginning of feudalism".

examAngle.point: Trade: ports such as Sopara, Kalyan, Bharuch, Ghantasala and Motupalli; coins with ships; trade with Rome fell after them.
examAngle.context: Satavahana lead and potin coins show ships, which is proof of sea trade with Rome. Craft guilds (**shrenis**) worked like banks and took deposits at about 12% a year. The **Kolika** guild was a guild of weavers. No later dynasty issued ship coins.

examAngle.point: Katakas and skandhavaras were army camps that also served as offices of government. Maharathis and Mahabhojas were feudatories (vassal chiefs); Amatyas were officers.
examAngle.context: The Satavahanas ruled a big land through army camps and local chiefs, not through a tight, Mauryan-style set of officials.

examAngle.point: Books of the age: Katantra Vyakaranam by Sarvavarma (a short Sanskrit grammar), and Lilavati Parinayam (Lilavai) by Kutuhala (Prakrit).
examAngle.context: Both show that Sanskrit and Prakrit learning grew together at the Satavahana court.

examAngle.point: They issued two-language coins (Prakrit and a Dravidian script) and supported both Buddhism and Vedic religion. They had no marriage tie with the Kakatiyas.
examAngle.context: The Kakatiyas came about 1,000 years later (1163 CE). This is a classic order trap. Use the pegs: Satavahanas about 230 BCE–225 CE; Kakatiyas 1163–1323 CE.

events.title: Bhattiprolu casket & Brahmi variant
events.summary: The Bhattiprolu stupa (Guntur, c. 200 BCE) has a relic casket inscription in an early southern form of Brahmi — the "Bhattiprolu script", ancestor of the Telugu script.
events.detail: Relic caskets with crystal containers were found here in 1870–92 by Boswell and Alexander Rea. The inscription mentions a king Kubiraka. Bhattiprolu shows that Buddhism and writing had reached the Krishna delta by the 2nd century BCE.
causes: Spread of Buddhism along the Krishna.
outcomes: Basis of the later Telugu–Kannada script.
events.yearHook: About 200 BCE, roughly 30 years after the Satavahanas begin (about 230 BCE).
events.before: Ashoka's monks (about 260 BCE) carried Buddhism and the **Brahmi** script down the Krishna river. Near the river mouth, at Bhattiprolu, local people built a **stupa**: a dome of brick and earth over relics (remains) of the Buddha.
events.after: The southern Brahmi letters of Bhattiprolu changed slowly over about 700 years into the **Telugu-Kannada script**. The first inscription written fully in Telugu comes at **Kalamalla**, about 575 CE, the last event of this lesson.
events.today: Bhattiprolu is a village in the Krishna delta, near Repalle. The relic caskets, with crystal containers inside, were dug out between 1870 and 1892 (by Boswell, then Alexander Rea).
events.mnemonic: Bhattiprolu = "Telugu script's grandmother": its letters slowly grew into the Telugu-Kannada script.

examAngle.point: Kubiraka (Kubhiraka) is named as the ruler of Bhattiprolu.
examAngle.context: He is one of the earliest local kings of Andhra known by name, from about the 3rd–2nd century BCE, as old as the first Satavahanas. The casket inscription names him as the king when the relics were enshrined.

events.title: Pushyamitra Shunga founds the Shunga dynasty
events.summary: Pushyamitra Shunga kills the last Maurya, Brihadratha (c. 185 BCE) (NCERT), founds the Shunga dynasty and revives Vedic sacrifices.
events.detail: Pushyamitra performed two ashvamedhas and fought the Indo-Greeks; Kalidasa's Malavikagnimitram has his son Agnimitra as hero. Patanjali wrote the Mahabhashya in this age. The Bharhut stupa railings date from Shunga times. The Kanvas (Vasudeva Kanva) replaced the Shungas about 73 BCE and were overthrown by the Satavahanas.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History I, Ch. 2 "Kings, Farmers and Towns"; Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)
causes: Weak later Mauryas.
outcomes: Shungas then Kanvas ruled Magadha; Bharhut stupa.

alsoOn.text: Vasudeva Kanva overthrows the last Shunga and founds the Kanva dynasty.

events.yearHook: c. 185 BCE (NCERT): end of the Mauryas.
facts: Later Shungas: Agnimitra, Vasumitra, Bhagabhadra, Devabhuti (last). Kanvas: Vasudeva, Bhumimitra, Narayana, Susharman (last).
Pushyamitra performed two Ashvamedha yagnas.
Parishishtaparvan (Hemachandra) is a Jaina source on this period.
The Yavana (Greek) invasion in Pushyamitra's time is mentioned in the Gargi Samhita, Patanjali's Mahabhashya and Kalidasa's Malavikagnimitra (not the Mudrarakshasa) (APPSC Group-1 key).

events.title: Indo-Greek invasions of the north-west
events.summary: Indo-Greek kings rule the north-west (c. 200–100 BCE) (NCERT); Menander (Milinda) is the best known, and they are the first to issue coins with kings' portraits and names.
events.detail: Demetrius invaded about 180 BCE. Menander ruled from Sakala (Sialkot); the Milindapanha records his questions to the monk Nagasena. The Heliodorus pillar at Besnagar (Vidisha) was set up by a Greek envoy who called himself a devotee of Vasudeva. Gandhara art later mixed Greek and Indian styles.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History I, Ch. 2 "Kings, Farmers and Towns"; Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)
causes: Weakness of the post-Mauryan north-west.
outcomes: Gold and portrait coins; Gandhara art; Heliodorus pillar.
facts: The Indo-Greeks came from Bactria; Indians called them Yavanas (Yona in Ashoka's RE-13).
Antialcidas sent Heliodorus to king Bhagabhadra of Vidisha (c. 113 BCE), who set up the Garuda pillar — evidence of Bhagavatism.
Menander I "Soter"; Strato II was among the last kings.
Their coins combined Greek deities + Indian symbols (such as the Dharmachakra).
They were followed by the Scythians (Shakas) and the Yuezhi (Kushanas).

events.title: Vikrama Samvat era begins
events.summary: The Vikram Samvat era begins in 57 BCE, traditionally after a king Vikramaditya of Ujjain drove out the Shakas.
events.detail: It is used in north and west India and is the official calendar of Nepal. The Saka era (78 CE) is India's national calendar, adopted in 1957.
causes: Tradition of victory over the Shakas.
outcomes: Still used in Hindu calendars.
events.yearHook: 57 BCE + 135 = 78 CE: Vikram to Saka era.

events.title: Araku Valley & Borra Caves (Eastern Ghats)
events.summary: Araku hill-station & the million-year-old Borra limestone caves (Alluri dist.).
events.detail:
Eastern Ghats tourism & tribal (Adivasi) belt.

**Exam hooks:** Borra Caves — karst limestone caves; Araku coffee (GI).

events.title: AP geography: coast, ghats & three regions
events.summary: AP = Coastal Andhra + Rayalaseema; ~1000 km coastline (2nd longest).
events.detail:
Bordered by the Bay of Bengal, Eastern Ghats & the Deccan plateau.

**Exam hooks:** AP coastline ~974 km (2nd after Gujarat); Kadapa/Nallamala hills.

events.title: Kolleru & Pulicat — AP's great lakes
events.summary: Kolleru (freshwater) & Pulicat (brackish lagoon) — key wetlands & bird habitats.
events.detail:
Kolleru bird sanctuary; Pulicat near Sriharikota.

**Exam hooks:** Pulicat = India's 2nd-largest brackish-water lagoon; Kolleru Ramsar debate.

events.title: Krishna & Godavari — AP's lifelines
events.summary: The Godavari (largest peninsular river) & Krishna define AP's deltas.
events.detail:
Both drain the Eastern Ghats to the Bay of Bengal.

**Exam hooks:** Godavari = "Dakshina Ganga"; deltas = the "rice bowl" (Konaseema).

events.title: Kanishka I; Saka era begins under the Kushanas
events.summary: Kanishka, the greatest Kushana king, comes to the throne (traditionally 78 CE, start of the Saka era); he patronises Mahayana Buddhism and the Gandhara and Mathura schools of art.
events.detail:
The Kushanas came from Central Asia; NCERT notes that their kings called themselves devaputra and that their colossal statues have been found at Mat near Mathura and in Afghanistan. Kanishka ruled from Purushapura (Peshawar) to Mathura and beyond.

The Fourth Buddhist Council in Kashmir under Vasumitra and Ashvaghosha marked the rise of Mahayana. His court had Ashvaghosha, Vasumitra and the physician Charaka. Kushana gold coins were the purest of ancient India.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History I, Ch. 2 "Kings, Farmers and Towns"; Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)
causes: Kushana migration from Central Asia.
outcomes: Mahayana Buddhism spread to Central Asia and China.
Gandhara and Mathura art schools.
facts: Kushana kings took the title devaputra (son of god) (NCERT).
Statues of Kushana kings found at Mat, Mathura (NCERT).
The Kushanas were a branch of the Yuezhi; Kujula Kadphises I founded the dynasty, Vima Kadphises II issued gold coins.
The Mahayana–Hinayana split became sharp after the Fourth Council.
Kushana power declined under Sassanian (Persian) pressure.
The Shakas and Kushanas introduced Central Asian dress: turban, trousers, heavy long coat, helmet and boots (APPSC Group-1 key); also better cavalry and the use of the saddle.
events.yearHook: 78 CE — start of the Saka era.

participants.role: Mahayana philosopher of the same age.
Physician at his court, by tradition.

events.title: Karikala Chola; Sangam kingdoms flourish
events.summary: Karikala, the greatest early Chola king, defeats the Cheras and Pandyas at Venni and is credited with the Kallanai dam on the Kaveri.
events.detail: Sangam poems praise him. His capital was Uraiyur and his port Puhar (Kaveripattinam), described in the Pattinappalai. The Grand Anicut (Kallanai) is one of the oldest working water structures.
causes: Rivalry of the three crowned kings of the Tamil land.
outcomes: Chola supremacy in the Sangam age.

events.title: Ashvaghosha writes Buddhacharita
events.summary: Ashvaghosha, poet at Kanishka's court, writes the Buddhacharita, a Sanskrit life of the Buddha.
events.detail:
Court poet of Kanishka.

**Exam hooks:** Buddhacharita & Saundarananda; Mahayana texts flourish.
causes: Kushana patronage of Buddhism.
outcomes: Mahayana texts began to be written in Sanskrit.

events.title: Gautamiputra Satakarni — Satavahana peak
events.summary: Gautamiputra Satakarni (c. 106–130 CE), the greatest Satavahana king, defeats the Shaka Nahapana; his mother's Nasik inscription calls him destroyer of the Shakas, Yavanas and Pahlavas (NCERT).
events.detail: He restruck Nahapana's silver coins with his own name. The Nasik inscription of Gautami Balashri calls him "ekabrahmana" and claims he stopped the mixing of the four varnas (NCERT). His successors fought Rudradaman.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History I, Ch. 2 "Kings, Farmers and Towns"
causes: Shaka expansion into the Deccan.
outcomes: Satavahana power restored.
gains: Western Deccan and Malwa recovered.
events.yearHook: About 106 CE: 28 years after the Shaka era begins (78 CE), the calendar now used as India's national calendar.

participants.role: Shaka ruler who fought his successors.

events.before: In the 1st century CE the **Shakas** (Western Kshatrapas), foreigners from Central Asia, took Satavahana lands in Maharashtra and Gujarat. Their king **Nahapana** ruled from near Nashik.
events.after:
Gautamiputra won back the west. But soon after, the Shaka king **Rudradaman** of Ujjain beat his successor twice. Rudradaman's **Junagadh inscription** (about 150 CE) says he spared the Satavahana king only because they were related by marriage.

The Satavahanas then moved their centre east, to Andhra, under **Vasishthiputra Pulumavi**. That is why the next big Satavahana site in this lesson is Amaravati.
events.today: A hoard of Nahapana's silver coins, stamped again with Gautamiputra's name, was found at **Jogalthembi** near Nashik. It is hard proof of his victory.
events.mnemonic: "GSS beat N": Gautamiputra Satakarni Smashed Nahapana.

examAngle.point: His mother Gautami Balashri's Nasik inscription calls him "ekabrahmana" and the destroyer of the Shakas, Yavanas and Pahlavas.
examAngle.context: A mother praising her son: this is why Satavahana kings carry their mothers' names. **Shakas** = Scythians; **Yavanas** = Greeks; **Pahlavas** = Parthians. These were the three foreign groups of the north-west and west. "Ekabrahmana" ("the unique Brahmana") shows he claimed to protect the order of the four varnas.

events.title: Amaravati Stupa (Mahachaitya) flourishes
events.summary: The great stupa at Amaravati (Dhanyakataka) on the Krishna is enlarged and decorated with fine limestone sculpture under the later Satavahanas (c. 150–200 CE) (NCERT).
events.detail:
Amaravati was a major Buddhist centre and the Satavahana eastern capital. Its marble-like slabs show the life of the Buddha (NCERT shows the departure from the palace, c. 200 CE).

NCERT tells its later fate: in 1854 Walter Elliot, Commissioner of Guntur, took sculpture panels to Madras; many pieces are now in Chennai, Kolkata and the British Museum, and the stupa itself was destroyed. Sanchi, "discovered" in 1818, survived because it was not taken apart (NCERT).
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History I, Ch. 4 "Thinkers, Beliefs and Buildings"; Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
causes: Satavahana and merchant patronage of Buddhism.
outcomes: Amaravati school of art; sculptures spread to museums (NCERT).

alsoOn.text: Walter Elliot, Commissioner of Guntur, removes Amaravati sculptures to Madras (NCERT).
Sanchi stupa is "discovered" (NCERT).

events.yearHook: About 150 CE, the same years as Rudradaman's Junagadh inscription (about 150 CE).
events.before: Buddhism had been in Andhra since Ashoka (about 260 BCE). When the Satavahanas made **Dhanyakataka** their eastern capital, rich traders and royal women paid to enlarge the old stupa there.
events.after: Its style, the **Amaravati school** of sculpture, spread to Nagarjunakonda, Sri Lanka and South-East Asia. It is one of three great art schools of the age, with Gandhara in the north-west and Mathura in the north.
events.today: Its carved panels are now in the Government Museum (Chennai), the Indian Museum (Kolkata) and the British Museum (London). The rest is in the site museum at Amaravati. AP's new capital is named after it.
events.mnemonic: Three art schools of the age: "GMA" = Gandhara (Greek style), Mathura (red stone), Amaravati (white limestone).

examAngle.point: Amaravati is the biggest stupa in AP: the Mahachaitya.
examAngle.context: "Mahachaitya" means "great shrine". APPSC lists other AP stupas with it: Bhattiprolu, Ghantasala, Jaggayyapeta, Nagarjunakonda, Salihundam, Bavikonda and Thotlakonda. Use the north-to-south memory trick on the Buddhist sites slide.

events.title: Ikshvakus rule from Vijayapuri (Nagarjunakonda)
events.summary: The Ikshvakus succeed the Satavahanas in the Krishna valley (c. 225 CE) with capital Vijayapuri (Nagarjunakonda), where royal women build great Buddhist monasteries.
events.detail:
Vasishthiputra Chamtamula founded the dynasty and performed Vedic sacrifices, while his sister Chamtisri and other queens patronised Buddhism. Nagarjunakonda had stupas, viharas, a stadium and a university; it is linked by tradition with Acharya Nagarjuna.

The site was submerged by the Nagarjunasagar reservoir; its monuments were moved to an island museum (1960s).
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
causes: Decline of the Satavahanas.
outcomes: Followed by the Pallavas, Salankayanas and Vishnukundins in Andhra.
events.yearHook: About 225 CE, when the Satavahanas end. The Ikshvakus last about 100 years (about 225–325 CE).
events.before: The last great Satavahana king, **Yajna Sri Satakarni**, died around 200 CE. Their feudatories (vassal chiefs) in the Krishna valley took over. One of them, **Vasishthiputra Chamtamula**, started the Ikshvaku line at **Vijayapuri** (Nagarjunakonda).
events.after: Around 300–325 CE the Ikshvakus were overthrown by the **Pallavas** (and the Abhiras). Then small dynasties held Andhra: the **Salankayanas** at Vengi (the next event), the Brihatphalayanas and the Anandagotrikas. After them came the **Vishnukundins** (from about 420 CE).
events.today: When the **Nagarjunasagar dam** (finished 1967) flooded the valley, Nagarjunakonda's monuments were moved to an island museum in the lake. The dam and the town are named after **Acharya Nagarjuna**.
events.mnemonic: Ikshvaku kings in order: "Very Very Easy Ride" = Vasishthiputra Chamtamula, Virapurushadatta, Ehuvala Chamtamula, Rudrapurushadatta.

examAngle.point: The kings performed Vedic sacrifices, while the queens and princesses funded Buddhism: Chamtisiri (Chamtamula's sister) and Shantisri.
examAngle.context: One family, two faiths. The men did Vedic sacrifices such as the ashvamedha for royal glory; the women built monasteries. A lay woman devotee (**upasika**) named **Bodhisiri** also built many shrines.

examAngle.point: Virapurushadatta's reign was the golden age of Buddhism in Andhra. The last king was Rudrapurushadatta.
examAngle.context: Use the "Very Very Easy Ride" memory trick: Chamtamula, Virapurushadatta, Ehuvala Chamtamula, Rudrapurushadatta. The golden age is the second king, the end is the fourth.

examAngle.point: The Puranas call them "Sri Parvatiyas". They married into the Shaka (Western Kshatrapa) family of Ujjain. Their inscriptions do NOT claim descent from the Ikshvakus of Ayodhya.
examAngle.context: "Sri Parvata" is the Nagarjunakonda–Srisailam hill country. The name "Ikshvaku" sounds like the family of Rama of Ayodhya, but their own records never say so. APPSC tests exactly this.

examAngle.point: The Manchikallu inscription of Pallava Simhavarman (in Prakrit) shows that the Pallavas replaced the Ikshvakus at Vijayapuri.
examAngle.context: This is how we know the Ikshvaku line ended: the next inscription in their old land belongs to a Pallava king. The early Pallavas began in the Krishna region before they moved south to Kanchi.

examAngle.point: Acharya Nagarjuna founded the Madhyamika school, taught the Prajnaparamita ideas, and wrote the Suhrillekha ("letter to a friend") to a Satavahana king.
examAngle.context: Tradition links him with Nagarjunakonda. He lived in the late Satavahana age, and his ideas grew strong in the Ikshvaku monasteries. Madhyamika and Mahayana Buddhism later spread to Tibet, China and Japan.

events.title: Close of the Sangam Age; Kalabhra interregnum
events.summary: The Sangam age ends around 300 CE; the Kalabhras then rule the Tamil country until the Pallavas and Pandyas revive in the sixth century.
events.detail: The Tamil epics Silappadikaram (Ilango Adigal, about Kannagi and Kovalan) and Manimekalai belong to the post-Sangam period. The Kalabhra period is sometimes called a "dark age" because of few sources.
causes: Kalabhra invasion.
outcomes: Pallavas of Kanchi and Pandyas of Madurai rose later.

events.title: Chandragupta I founds the Gupta Empire
events.summary: Chandragupta I begins Gupta rule (c. 320 CE) (NCERT), marries the Lichchhavi princess Kumaradevi and takes the title Maharajadhiraja; the Gupta era starts in 319–320 CE.
events.detail: The Guptas began as a small family in the Ganga valley. Gold coins show Chandragupta I with Kumaradevi, showing the value of the Lichchhavi alliance. NCERT notes that Gupta history is built from literature, coins and inscriptions, including prashastis.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History I, Ch. 2 "Kings, Farmers and Towns"
causes: Marriage alliance with the Lichchhavis.
outcomes: Samudragupta's conquests (NCERT).

events.title: Samudragupta; Allahabad Prashasti
events.summary: Samudragupta (c. 335–375 CE) conquers widely; his court poet Harisena records it in the Prayaga prashasti on the Allahabad pillar (NCERT).
events.detail:
NCERT quotes the prashasti: he uprooted the kings of Aryavarta, captured and then freed twelve rulers of Dakshinapatha (including Vishnugopa of Kanchi and kings in coastal Andhra such as Hastivarman of Vengi), made forest kings his servants, and took tribute from frontier states and the Shakas and Kushanas.

His coins show him playing the veena. The same pillar has an Ashokan edict and a Jahangir inscription. V.A. Smith called him the "Napoleon of India".
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History I, Ch. 2 "Kings, Farmers and Towns"
causes: Gupta ambition to unify the north.
gains: Aryavarta annexed; the south made tributary.
outcomes: Gupta empire at its height.
facts: Prayaga prashasti by Harisena (NCERT).
Kings of Dakshinapatha were captured and released (grahana-moksha-anugraha).
Gupta founders: Sri Gupta and Ghatotkacha before Chandragupta I.

participants.role: The same pillar carries his edict.
His inscription is on the same pillar.

events.title: Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya)
events.summary: Chandragupta II Vikramaditya (c. 375–415 CE) (NCERT) ends Shaka rule in western India; Kalidasa, Fa-Hien's visit and the Mehrauli iron pillar belong to his age.
events.detail:
He defeated the last Western Kshatrapa and took Gujarat with its ports, issuing silver coins. His daughter Prabhavati married the Vakataka king, securing the Deccan (NCERT notes the Vakatakas c. 375–415 CE).

The Mehrauli iron pillar, which has not rusted, records a king Chandra. By tradition nine gems (navaratnas) — Kalidasa, Amarasimha, Varahamihira, Dhanvantari and others — adorned his court.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History I, Ch. 2 "Kings, Farmers and Towns"
causes: Shaka control of the western coast.
gains: Gujarat, Saurashtra and Malwa.
outcomes: Gupta "golden age" of art and literature.

participants.role: One of the nine gems, by tradition.

facts: Gupta administration: bhukti (province), vishaya (district), vithi, grama; shrenis (guilds); gold coins called dinaras.
Sultanganj Buddha (copper) is a Gupta masterpiece; Devichandragupta (Vishakhadatta) tells of Ramagupta.
Gupta guilds (shrenis) were autonomous bodies: they had their own seals and coins, kept armed bands and worked as bankers (APPSC Group-1 key).

events.title: Fa-Hien travels through Gupta India
events.summary: The Chinese monk Fa-Hien travels in India (c. 399–414 CE) in Chandragupta II's reign, collecting Buddhist texts, and describes a peaceful, prosperous land.
events.detail: He came overland through Central Asia and returned by sea via Sri Lanka. He noted free hospitals in Pataliputra, light taxes, and that Chandalas (untouchables) lived outside towns and had to strike a piece of wood to announce themselves.
causes: Search for Buddhist texts.
outcomes: His record is a key source for the Guptas.

events.title: Vishnukundins rule coastal Andhra
events.summary: The Vishnukundins rule coastal Andhra and Telangana (c. 420–620 CE); Madhava Varma I makes them powerful, and they build the Undavalli and Mogalrajapuram cave temples.
events.detail: They worshipped Sri Parvata Swami (Srisailam) and performed Vedic sacrifices. Capitals included Indrapalanagara (Nalgonda) and later Amarapura/Denduluru. The Undavalli caves near Vijayawada have a reclining Vishnu. They were overthrown by the Badami Chalukya Pulakeshin II, whose brother founded the Eastern Chalukya line in Vengi (624 CE).
causes: Decline of the Ikshvakus and Salankayanas.
outcomes: Replaced by the Eastern Chalukyas (624 CE).
