events.yearHook: About 420 CE to 624 CE. They end the year Pulakeshin II takes Vengi (624).
events.before: After the Salankayanas and Samudragupta's raid, the **Vishnukundins** rose in the hills of Telangana (capital **Indrapalanagara**, Nalgonda) and spread down to coastal Andhra.
events.after: **Pulakeshin II** of Badami defeated them. In 624 CE he gave Vengi to his brother **Kubja Vishnuvardhana**. That began the **Eastern Chalukyas**, who made Telugu a language of the court. That is the start of lesson 2.
events.today: The **Undavalli caves** (near Vijayawada, on the Krishna) with a 5-metre reclining Vishnu, and the **Mogalrajapuram caves** in Vijayawada, are open to visitors.
events.mnemonic: Vishnukundins = "V to V": they begin in the hills of Telangana and end at Vengi.

examAngle.point: Madhava Varma had the title "Janasraya" and moved the capital from Amarapuri to Denduluru.
examAngle.context: Denduluru is near Eluru, close to old Vengi. The move brought the kingdom down from the hills to the rich delta.

examAngle.point: They issued iron coins with a thin coating of copper, often with a lion on them.
examAngle.context: Such coated coins are rare in India. The lion was their royal emblem.

examAngle.point: Historian N. Venkataramanaiah identified their family god, "Sri Parvata Swami", with the Buddha.
examAngle.context: Most historians see Sri Parvata Swami as **Shiva of Srisailam**. But APPSC 2018 keyed Venkataramanaiah's view. Learn both: Shiva is the usual view; the Buddha is his view.

events.title: Nalanda Mahavihara flourishes
events.summary: Kumaragupta I founds the Buddhist monastery-university at Nalanda (c. 427 CE); it later draws students from China, Korea and Tibet.
events.detail: Xuanzang studied there under Shilabhadra and said it had 10,000 students and teachers. It was supported by the revenue of many villages. Harsha and the Pala kings patronised it. Bakhtiyar Khalji destroyed it about 1193. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
causes: Gupta patronage of learning.
outcomes: Asia's greatest centre of Buddhist learning.
events.yearHook: About 427 CE under the Gupta king Kumaragupta I; destroyed about 1193 — some 750 years of learning.
events.before: Monasteries had been places of study since the Mauryan age. Under the **Guptas** large monastery-universities grew with land grants from kings.
events.after: Harsha (7th century) and the **Pala** kings of Bengal (8th–12th century) supported it; the Palas also founded **Vikramashila**. **Bakhtiyar Khalji** destroyed both about 1193, which hastened Buddhism's decline.
events.today: The ruins are a UNESCO World Heritage Site (2016). A new Nalanda University opened nearby at Rajgir (2014).

events.title: Skandagupta repels Hunas; Gupta decline
events.summary: Skandagupta (c. 455–467 CE) repels the first Huna invasion, but after him the Gupta empire declines through Huna attacks, weak rulers and rising feudatories.
events.detail: His Bhitari pillar records the Huna war; his Junagadh inscription records repairs to the Sudarshana lake. Toramana and Mihirakula later took the north-west. Feudatories such as the Maukharis of Kanauj and the Maitrakas of Valabhi broke away. Gupta rule ended about 550 CE.
causes: Huna invasions.
Rise of feudatories.
outcomes: Regional kingdoms; later Harsha united the north.

participants.role: Huna king who took the north-west.

events.title: Pulakeshin I founds the Chalukyas of Badami
events.summary: Pulakeshin I founds the Chalukya dynasty of Badami (Vatapi) in Karnataka (c. 543 CE) (NCERT notes the rise of the Chalukyas c. 500–600 CE).
events.detail: He performed the ashvamedha and fortified Vatapi. His successors Kirtivarman I and Mangalesha expanded the kingdom; the cave temples of Badami were cut under them. Pulakeshin II became the greatest king.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History I, Ch. 2 "Kings, Farmers and Towns"; Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)
causes: Decline of the Vakatakas and Kadambas.
outcomes: Chalukya–Pallava rivalry.

events.title: Aihole–Badami temple architecture
events.summary: The Chalukyas build early stone temples at Aihole, Badami and Pattadakal; Aihole is called the "cradle of Indian temple architecture".
events.detail: The Lad Khan and Durga temples at Aihole are experiments in temple form. Pattadakal (UNESCO) has temples in both northern (nagara) and southern (dravida) styles; the Virupaksha temple was built by queen Lokamahadevi. In Kanchi the Pallava Mahendravarman I began rock-cut temples.
causes: Chalukya and Pallava patronage.
outcomes: Nagara and dravida styles developed side by side.
facts: Meguti Jain temple, Aihole, carries the Aihole inscription (634 CE).
Temple styles: Nagara (north), Dravidian (south, with vimana), Vesara (mixed, Deccan).

events.title: Harshavardhana ascends; capital at Kanauj
events.summary: Harshavardhana becomes king of Thanesar and Kanauj (606 CE) (NCERT) after his brother Rajyavardhana is killed; his reign is described by Banabhatta and Xuanzang.
events.detail:
His sister Rajyashri had married the Maukhari king of Kanauj, who was killed by the king of Malwa; Rajyavardhana was then killed by Shashanka of Gauda. Harsha rescued Rajyashri and made Kanauj his capital.

The Harshacharita of Banabhatta is a biography in Sanskrit (NCERT). Harsha wrote the plays Ratnavali, Nagananda and Priyadarshika. The Harsha era begins in 606 CE.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History I, Ch. 2 "Kings, Farmers and Towns"
causes: Murder of his brother by Shashanka.
outcomes: Harsha ruled much of the north for 41 years.
facts: Harsha was a Vardhana (Pushyabhuti); ally of Bhaskaravarman of Kamarupa (Assam).
Administration: bhukti (province), vishaya (district), grama (village); tax bali and bhaga.
Harsha sent an embassy to China (c. 641); traditionally his first campaigns c. 618–619 CE.

events.title: Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi in Andhra
events.summary: Pulakeshin II conquers Vengi in coastal Andhra and makes his brother Kubja Vishnuvardhana its ruler (624 CE), founding the Eastern Chalukya dynasty that rules for about 450 years.
events.detail: The capital moved from Pishtapura (Pithapuram) to Vengi and later Rajamahendravaram (Rajahmundry). The Eastern Chalukyas fought the Rashtrakutas and later allied with the Cholas by marriage. Telugu literature began under Rajaraja Narendra with Nannaya's Mahabharata (11th century).
causes: Pulakeshin II's conquest of the Vishnukundin lands.
outcomes: Eastern Chalukya rule; merger with the Cholas (Chalukya-Cholas, 1070).
events.yearHook: 624 CE — ten years before the Aihole inscription.

participants.role: Poet at the Eastern Chalukya court.

facts: Pulakeshin II's Marturu inscription calls Mangalagiri "Mangalapura" (APPSC Group-II 2018 key).
Chellavva received the title "Gandharva-Vidya-Visarada" (expert in music and dance) (APPSC Group-II 2018 key).
Ugradityacharya wrote the medical work "Kalyanakaraka" (APPSC Group-II 2018 key).
Vijayaditya II is said to have built 108 Saiva temples; Vijayaditya III developed Kandukuru on the lines of Bezawada (APPSC Group-II 2018 key).
The early Chalukyas worshipped the mother-goddess Hariti; the Kapalikas emerged from the Misra Saivam school (APPSC Group-II 2018 key).
Penugonda (West Godavari) is the main seat of goddess Vasavi (Kanyaka Parameswari) (APPSC Group-II 2018 key).
Ayyana Mahadevi, queen of Kubja Vishnuvardhana, built the Jaina temple "Nedumba Vasati" near Vijayawada (APPSC Group-II 2025 key).

Royal marriages: Vimaladitya (not Saktivarma) married Kundavai, daughter of Rajaraja Chola I; Rajaraja Narendra married Ammangadevi, daughter of Rajendra Chola I; Rajendra Chalukya (Kulottunga I) married Madhurantaki, daughter of Rajendra Chola II (APPSC Group-II 2025 key).

Vijayaditya II is credited with 108 temples; Chalukya Bhima built the Bhimeswara Swamy temple at Draksharama; the Rajarajeswara temple at Biccavole was NOT built by Rajaraja Narendra (APPSC Group-II 2025 key).
The Draksharama temple shows the independent Chalukya-Chola style, with Pallava and early Chalukya influences (APPSC Group-II 2025 key).

The credit for establishing Telugu as a language of administration and literature in Andhradesa goes to the Eastern Chalukyas — Telugu inscriptions multiply (Addanki, Dharmavaram) and Nannaya wrote under Rajaraja Narendra (APPSC Group-II Screening 2018 key).

events.title: Hiuen Tsang at Harsha's court
events.summary: Xuanzang (Hiuen Tsang) travels in India (c. 629–645 CE) in search of Buddhist texts (NCERT), studies at Nalanda and writes the Si-yu-ki (Records of the Western World).
events.detail: He visited Harsha's court, attended the assemblies at Kanauj and Prayaga (643 CE), visited Pulakeshin II's kingdom, Kanchi and Andhra, including Dhanyakataka (Amaravati), where he found Buddhism declining. He returned with 657 texts.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History I, Ch. 2 "Kings, Farmers and Towns"
causes: Search for Buddhist texts (NCERT).
outcomes: Si-yu-ki is a major source for 7th-century India.
facts: Xuanzang travelled 629/630–643/645 CE.
I-Tsing (Yijing) visited 671–695 CE and studied at Nalanda.
Later Chinese visitors: Ma Huan with Zheng He's fleets (15th century).

events.title: Pulakeshin II checks Harsha on the Narmada
events.summary: Pulakeshin II stops Harsha on the banks of the Narmada; the Aihole inscription (634 CE), written by Ravikirti, records the victory (NCERT).
events.detail: Harsha, "lord of the north" (Uttarapathapati), tried to expand south. Pulakeshin II, "lord of the south" (Dakshinapathapati), defeated him; Ravikirti says Harsha's joy melted away when he saw his elephants fall. The Narmada became the boundary between the two.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History I, Ch. 2 "Kings, Farmers and Towns"
causes: Harsha's southern expansion.
losses: Harsha's army and elephants.
outcomes: Narmada fixed as the frontier.
facts: Aihole inscription by Ravikirti, dated 634 CE (NCERT).

events.title: Pallava Narasimhavarman I sacks Vatapi
events.summary: The Pallava king Narasimhavarman I defeats and kills Pulakeshin II and captures Vatapi (642 CE), taking the title "Vatapikonda".
events.detail: Mahendravarman I had lost land to Pulakeshin II. His son Narasimhavarman I, called Mamalla, took revenge with the help of the Sri Lankan prince Manavarma. He built the monolithic rathas (Pancha Rathas) at Mamallapuram (Mahabalipuram). The Chalukyas recovered under Vikramaditya I.
causes: Chalukya–Pallava rivalry; Pulakeshin II's earlier victories.
losses: Pulakeshin II killed; Vatapi sacked.
outcomes: Pallava supremacy for 13 years.
events.yearHook: 642 CE — eight years after the Aihole inscription.

participants.role: His father, who had lost to Pulakeshin.

events.title: Death of Harsha; his empire disintegrates
events.summary: Harsha dies in 647 CE without an heir; his empire breaks up, and Kanauj becomes the prize for which later dynasties fight.
events.detail: In 643 CE Harsha held a great assembly at Kanauj in honour of Xuanzang and a quinquennial gift-giving at Prayaga, where he gave away his wealth. After his death a minister seized the throne; the tripartite struggle for Kanauj followed in the 8th century.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History I, Ch. 2 "Kings, Farmers and Towns"
causes: No heir.
outcomes: Political fragmentation of the north; later the tripartite struggle.

alsoOn.text: Harsha holds assemblies at Kanauj and Prayaga in honour of Xuanzang.

events.title: Rashtrakutas dominate the Deccan
events.summary: Dantidurga overthrows the Chalukyas of Badami and founds the Rashtrakuta dynasty (c. 753 CE) (NCERT); Krishna I builds the Kailasa temple at Ellora.
events.detail:
NCERT notes that Dantidurga, a Chalukya subordinate, performed the hiranyagarbha ("golden womb") ritual so that he would be "reborn" a Kshatriya. Rashtrakuta capital later moved to Manyakheta.

Krishna I carved the Kailasanatha temple at Ellora out of a single rock. Amoghavarsha I wrote the Kavirajamarga, the earliest Kannada work on poetics. The Rashtrakutas fought the Palas and Pratiharas for Kanauj and the Eastern Chalukyas for Vengi.
events.source: NCERT Class 7 Our Pasts II; Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)
causes: Weak later Chalukyas.
outcomes: A Deccan power for 200 years; replaced by the Chalukyas of Kalyani (973).
facts: Krishna I (not Krishna III) built the Kailasa temple at Ellora (APPSC Group-1 key). Amoghavarsha I wrote the Kavirajamarga, the first Kannada book on poetics; the Arab traveller Al-Masudi called the Rashtrakuta king "Vallabharaja" (Balhara).
Ellora caves in order of building (APPSC key): Dashavatara (cave 15), Ravan ki Khai, Dumar Lena, then the Kailasanatha. Ellora has Buddhist (1–12), Hindu (13–29) and Jaina (30–34) caves.

events.title: Tripartite struggle for Kanauj
events.summary: The Gurjara-Pratiharas, Rashtrakutas and Palas fight for control of Kanauj in the Ganga valley for about 200 years — the "tripartite struggle" (NCERT).
events.detail:
Kanauj had been Harsha's capital and was the symbol of power in the north. NCERT explains that the three dynasties fought for it over centuries. The Pala Dharmapala placed his nominee there; the Pratihara Nagabhata II captured it (c. 816); the Rashtrakutas raided the north several times.

The Pratiharas, under Mihira Bhoja, finally held Kanauj and also stopped the Arabs of Sind. The long war exhausted all three.
causes: Prestige and wealth of Kanauj (NCERT).
outcomes: All three weakened; regional Rajput kingdoms rose.
facts: Pratihara kings: Vatsaraja, Nagabhata II, Mihira Bhoja; they claimed the Agnikula myth (born from fire).
Other Rajput kingdoms: Paramaras (Bhoja built Bhojeshwar temple), Chaulukyas/Solankis (Bhimadeva I faced Mahmud), Gahadavalas of Kannauj (Jaichandra), Tomaras of Delhi (Dhillika, Lal Kot).
Dharmapala called himself Sakalottarapathanatha (lord of the north); he founded Vikramshila.

events.title: Imperial Cholas rise; Rajaraja I
events.summary: Rajaraja I becomes Chola king (985), builds a navy, conquers Sri Lanka and the Maldives, and builds the Brihadeshvara temple at Thanjavur (NCERT).
events.detail:
The Cholas rose from Uraiyur when Vijayalaya captured Thanjavur (mid-9th century) (NCERT). Rajaraja I was the most powerful early Chola ruler and reorganised the administration (NCERT).

Chola villages were run by sabhas (brahmana assemblies) and urs (non-brahmana villages); the Uttaramerur inscriptions describe how sabha members were chosen by lot (NCERT). Chola bronzes, such as the Nataraja, are world famous (NCERT).
causes: Chola conquest of the Kaveri delta (NCERT).
outcomes: Chola empire across the south and Sri Lanka.
Brihadeshvara temple (1010) (NCERT).
facts: Uttaramerur inscriptions describe the sabha (NCERT).
Chola bronzes made by the lost-wax technique (NCERT).
Land grants: brahmadeya (to brahmanas), devadana (to temples), shalabhoga, vellanvagai.
Village assemblies chose members by kudavolai (pot-ticket lots) and worked through variyams (committees).
Dravidian temples have a tall vimana over the shrine; Brihadeeswara (Thanjavur); Nataraja bronzes are a high point of Dravidian art.

The imperial Chola dynasty was founded by Vijayalaya, not Parantaka I; Parantaka I took the title Maduraikondan ("conqueror of Madurai"); Rajaraja I conquered the Maldive islands; Rajendra I built Gangaikonda Cholapuram (APPSC Group-1 key).
Chola village terms: variyam = committee; kudumba = ward; kudavolai = lottery system; perumakkal = member of the village assembly (APPSC Group-1 key).

events.title: Tirumala–Tirupati temple tradition
events.summary: The Venkateswara temple at Tirumala grows into a great pilgrimage centre, patronised by the Pallavas, Cholas, Telugu Chodas and later Vijayanagara kings.
events.detail: Inscriptions from Pallava queen Samavai (966 CE) record gifts. Ramanuja is said to have organised the worship. Krishnadevaraya visited seven times and placed statues of himself and his queens there. Annamacharya wrote thousands of kirtanas on Venkateswara. TTD now administers it.
causes: Royal and popular patronage.
outcomes: One of the world's most visited shrines.

events.title: Mahmud of Ghazni raids Somnath
events.summary: Mahmud of Ghazni raids the subcontinent 17 times between 1000 and 1025 (NCERT); in 1025 he plunders the Somnath temple in Gujarat.
events.detail:
Mahmud ruled from Ghazni in Afghanistan. His targets were wealthy temples, including Somnath (NCERT). He used the wealth to build a splendid capital at Ghazni. He defeated the Hindushahi ruler Jayapala (1001) and Anandapala.

He was interested in learning about the people he conquered and asked Al-Biruni to write an account of the subcontinent (NCERT).
causes: Plunder of temple wealth (NCERT).
course: 1000: first raid.
1001: defeats Jayapala near Peshawar.
1018: Mathura and Kanauj.
1025: Somnath (NCERT).
losses: Temples plundered; Somnath destroyed.
outcomes: Punjab became a Ghaznavid province.
Al-Biruni's Kitab-ul-Hind (NCERT).

events.title: Nannaya begins the Telugu Mahabharatam
events.summary: At the request of the Eastern Chalukya king Rajaraja Narendra, Nannaya begins the Telugu Mahabharata at Rajahmundry (11th century), starting Telugu literature.
events.detail: Nannaya, called the "Adikavi", translated the Adi and Sabha parvas and part of the Aranya parva. He also wrote Andhra Shabda Chintamani, the first Telugu grammar (in Sanskrit). Rajaraja Narendra ruled from Rajamahendravaram.
causes: Royal patronage of Telugu.
outcomes: Tikkana and Errana completed the work (Kavitrayam).
events.yearHook: c. 1050 — about 1,000 years of Telugu literature.
facts: Pavuluri Mallana wrote "Sarasangraha Ganitam", a mathematical work in Telugu (APPSC Group-II 2018 key).
Nannaya wrote the Andhra Mahabharatam and the Andhra Shabda Chintamani (a Sanskrit treatise on Telugu grammar) (APPSC Group-II 2025 key).
Pavuluri Mallana — Ganitasara Sangraham; Vinukonda Vallabharaya — Kreedabhiramam (APPSC Group-II 2025 key).

The Nandampudi grant of Rajaraja Narendra (1053) is the evidence that Narayana Bhatta assisted Nannaya in translating the Mahabharata; it was composed by Nannaya himself (APPSC Group-II Screening 2018 key).

events.title: Simhachalam & Andhra temple architecture
events.summary: The Varaha-Lakshmi Narasimha temple at Simhachalam near Visakhapatnam is rebuilt in the Kalinga style; the Eastern Ganga king Narasimhadeva I adds to it (13th century).
events.detail: Inscriptions go back to the 11th century (Kulottunga I). The Eastern Gangas of Kalinga, who built Konark, rebuilt it; Krishnadevaraya visited after his Kalinga campaign (1516). The deity is covered in sandal paste except on Akshaya Tritiya (Chandanotsavam).
causes: Royal patronage.
outcomes: Major Vaishnava shrine of north coastal Andhra.

participants.role: Earliest inscriptions date from his reign.

events.title: Kakatiyas assert independence at Warangal
events.summary: The Kakatiya chief Rudradeva declares independence from the Chalukyas of Kalyani (c. 1163); the Anumakonda inscription records it, and he builds the Thousand Pillar temple.
events.detail: The Kakatiyas began as feudatories at Anumakonda (Hanamkonda). Prola II resisted the Chalukyas; his son Rudradeva (Prataparudra I) became independent and began the Warangal fort. The Kakatiyas brought the Telugu lands under one rule for the first time and built thousands of tanks for irrigation.
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
causes: Decline of the Kalyani Chalukyas.
outcomes: Kakatiya kingdom until 1323.
facts: The Thousand Pillar temple is also called the Rudreshwara temple (Hanumakonda), built 1163.
Kakatiyas ruled c. 1163–1323; Ganapatideva–Rudramadevi–Prataparudra.
Prolaraja I constructed the Kesari Samudram tank (APPSC Group-II 2018 key).
Pradvivaka was the king's adviser on judiciary (APPSC Group-II 2018 key).

Early Kakatiya kings built Jaina temples; Kalyani Chalukya influence is seen in Kakatiya temples; the Thousand Pillar temple is "trikuta" — three shrines to Rudreshwara, Vasudeva and Suryadeva (APPSC Group-II 2025 key).
Inscriptions: Sanigaram — Prolaraja; Anumakonda — Rudradeva; Bayyaram — Mailamba; Motupalli — Ganapatideva (APPSC Group-II 2025 key).
Prolaraja bore the title Arikesari; Beta II was initiated into Saivism by Rameswara Pandita of Srisailam; the Nayankara system was NOT introduced by Prataparudra (APPSC Group-II 2025 key).
Under the Kakatiyas the non-Brahmanisation of religion and politics culminated: Sudra rulers, Veerashaiva/Pasupata influence and non-Brahmin warrior nayakas (APPSC Group-II Screening 2018 key).

events.title: Second Battle of Tarain
events.summary: Prithviraj Chauhan defeats Muhammad Ghori in the First Battle of Tarain (1191) but loses the Second Battle of Tarain (1192) (NCERT), opening north India to Turkish rule.
events.detail: Tarain is near Thanesar in Haryana. In 1191 Prithviraj's army routed Ghori, who was wounded. Ghori returned in 1192 with mounted archers and a better plan; Prithviraj was defeated and killed. In 1194 Ghori defeated Jaichand of Kanauj at Chandawar. Ghori left Qutbuddin Aibak to rule his Indian conquests.
causes: Ghurid expansion into India.
course: 1191: First Battle — Ghori defeated (NCERT).
1192: Second Battle — Prithviraj defeated (NCERT).
1194: Battle of Chandawar — Jaichand defeated.
losses: Prithviraj killed (1192).
gains: Delhi and Ajmer for the Ghurids.
outcomes: Delhi Sultanate (1206).

alsoOn.text: First Battle of Tarain: Prithviraj Chauhan defeats Muhammad Ghori (NCERT).
Battle of Chandawar: Ghori defeats Jaichand of Kanauj.

events.title: Ganapati Deva — greatest Kakatiya
events.summary: Ganapati Deva (1199–1262), the greatest Kakatiya king, unites the Telugu lands, moves the capital to Warangal (Orugallu) and protects sea trade at Motupalli.
events.detail: His Motupalli abhaya-shasana (charter) promised safety and fair duties to foreign merchants. His general Recharla Rudra built the Ramappa temple (1213, UNESCO 2021) and the Ramappa lake. He extended the kingdom to Kanchi. Having no son, he named his daughter Rudramadevi heir.
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
causes: Kakatiya expansion.
outcomes: Warangal became a great capital; Ramappa temple.
facts: Kakatiya trade routes included Motupalli–Tripurantakam–Ballari and Palnadu–Nalgonda–Nekarikallu–Orugallu (APPSC Group-1 key).
Motupalli was also called Desiyakkonda Pattanam (APPSC Group-II 2018 key).
Kakatiya caste associations were called Samayamu; the Chitrameli guild was formed by agriculturists (APPSC Group-II 2018 key).
Pedaganjam and Chinaganjam were known for salt (APPSC Group-II 2018 key).
Jayana (Jayapa), author of Nrittaratnavali, was by profession a Gaja-Sahini (commander of elephants) (APPSC Group-II 2018 key).
The musical instrument Jalakaranda is mentioned in the Dharmasagar inscription (APPSC Group-II 2018 key).

events.title: Bhakti–Sufi movements spread
events.summary: Bhakti (devotion) and Sufi movements spread across India from about the 12th–13th centuries, building on the Alvars and Nayanars of Tamil Nadu (NCERT).
events.detail:
The Alvars (devotees of Vishnu) and Nayanars (devotees of Shiva) of the 6th–9th centuries sang in Tamil and came from all castes (NCERT). Ramanuja (11th–12th century) taught Vishishtadvaita and inspired Ramananda in the north (NCERT). Basavanna led the Virashaivas in Karnataka (NCERT).

Sufi silsilas such as the Chishtis (Muinuddin Chishti at Ajmer, Nizamuddin Auliya at Delhi) reached India in the 12th century (NCERT). Later saints include Kabir, Guru Nanak, Mirabai, Tulsidas and Chaitanya; in Andhra, Annamacharya, Potana and Ramadasu.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History II, Ch. 6 "Bhakti-Sufi Traditions"
causes: Reaction to ritualism and caste (NCERT).
outcomes: Literature in regional languages; new communities such as the Sikhs (NCERT).
facts: Nirguna bhakti (formless God: Kabir, Nanak) and Saguna bhakti (God with form: Tulsidas, Surdas, Mira).

Sufi terms: silsilah (order), pir (master), murid (disciple), khanqah (hospice), zikr (remembrance), sama (music), fanaa (passing away in God), maqamat (stages); wahdat-ul-wujud (unity of being) of Ibn Arabi.
Sheikh Ahmad Sirhindi (Naqshbandi) opposed it; Miyan Mir (Qadiri) laid the Golden Temple foundation, by tradition.
The southern teachers were called Acharyas; Lingayats wear the Ishtalinga.
Kabir wrote dohas; Sikh principles: Naam Japna, Kirat Karna (honest work), Vand Chhakna (sharing).
Varkari pilgrims of Maharashtra worship Vithoba (Vitthala) at Pandharpur.

events.title: Qutb-ud-din Aibak founds the Slave dynasty
events.summary: After Ghori's death Qutbuddin Aibak becomes the first Sultan of Delhi (1206–1210) (NCERT), founding the Mamluk ("Slave") dynasty.
events.detail:
Delhi first became an important city under the Tomara Rajputs, then the Chauhans; it became the capital of the Sultanate under the Turks (NCERT). Aibak had been a slave of Ghori. He began the Qutb Minar and the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque, and built the Adhai Din ka Jhonpra at Ajmer. He died after falling from his horse while playing polo (1210).

The Sultanate had five dynasties: Mamluk, Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid and Lodi (NCERT, Table 1).
causes: Ghori's death (1206).
outcomes: Delhi Sultanate 1206–1526 (NCERT).
facts: Ziauddin Barani wrote Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi; the Chihalgani (Chahalgani) were the Forty; Ranthambore was taken by Iltutmish and later Alauddin; Bahlol (Bahlul) Lodi founded the Lodis.

events.title: Iltutmish consolidates the Sultanate
events.summary: Iltutmish (1211–1236) consolidates the Delhi Sultanate, gets recognition from the Abbasid Caliph (1229), issues the silver tanka and copper jital, and organises the iqta system.
events.detail: He was Aibak's slave and son-in-law. He crushed rivals Yalduz and Qubacha, kept the Mongols away by refusing refuge to Jalaluddin Mangbarni, completed the Qutb Minar and formed the group of forty nobles (Chahalgani). He named his daughter Raziyya as heir (NCERT).
causes: Weak rule of Aram Shah.
outcomes: Sultanate made stable; Raziyya succeeded (1236) (NCERT).

events.title: Razia Sultana — first woman ruler of Delhi
events.summary: Raziyya, daughter of Iltutmish, becomes Sultan in 1236 and is removed in 1240 (NCERT) — the only woman Sultan of Delhi.
events.detail: NCERT says she was more able and qualified than her brothers, but the nobles were not happy with her attempts to rule independently. The chronicler Minhaj-i Siraj thought a queen went against the social order. NCERT contrasts her with Rudramadevi, who ruled successfully in Warangal.
causes: Iltutmish's choice of his daughter as heir (NCERT).
outcomes: Nobles (the Forty) dominated until Balban.

participants.role: One of the Forty; later Sultan.

events.title: Rani Rudrama Devi rules the Kakatiyas
events.summary: Rudramadevi rules the Kakatiya kingdom of Warangal (1262–1289) (NCERT), defeating the Yadavas and putting down rebel nobles.
events.detail: NCERT notes that she changed her name on inscriptions and pretended to be a man, taking a male royal title. She completed the Warangal fort and promoted the Nayankara system of military chiefs. Marco Polo praised her rule. She was succeeded by her grandson Prataparudra II.
events.source: NCERT Class 7 Our Pasts II; Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
causes: Ganapati Deva had no son.
outcomes: Kakatiya power held; Prataparudra II succeeded (1289).
facts: Rudramadevi bore the title "Rayagaja Kesari" for her victory over the rulers of Devagiri (Yadavas) (APPSC Group-II 2018 key).

events.title: Amir Khusrau — "Parrot of India"
events.summary: Amir Khusrau, poet and disciple of Nizamuddin Auliya, writes in Persian and Hindavi at the courts of the Khalji Sultans (from about 1290).
events.detail: He served seven Sultans from Balban to Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq. NCERT quotes him (1318) noting that every region had its own language. He is credited with developing qawwali and instruments such as the sitar (by tradition), and wrote Khazain-ul-Futuh on Alauddin's conquests.
causes: Court patronage.
outcomes: Hindavi literature; Indo-Persian music.

events.title: Alauddin Khilji; market & revenue reforms
events.summary: Alauddin Khalji becomes Sultan (1296–1316) after murdering his uncle Jalaluddin; he repels the Mongols, controls market prices and raids the south through Malik Kafur (NCERT).
events.detail:
NCERT describes his measures: he raised a large standing army paid in cash, and to feed it fixed the prices of goods in Delhi, with strict officers. He built a garrison town called Siri. He collected tax on land at half the produce.

His generals took Gujarat (1299), Ranthambhor (1301), Chittor (1303) and Devagiri, and Malik Kafur raided Warangal (1309), Dwarasamudra and Madurai.
causes: Mongol threat; need for a big army (NCERT).
outcomes: Sultanate reached the far south.
Market control ended after his death.

events.title: Fall of the Kakatiyas; Prataparudra captured
events.summary: Ulugh Khan (later Muhammad bin Tughlaq) captures Warangal (1323), ending the Kakatiya dynasty; Prataparudra II dies on the way to Delhi.
events.detail: A first Tughlaq attack in 1321 failed. In 1323 Warangal fell after a siege and was renamed Sultanpur. The 77 Nayakas who served the Kakatiyas soon led revolts; the Musunuri Nayakas freed Telangana (c. 1336), and the Reddis rose in coastal Andhra.
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
causes: Prataparudra stopped paying tribute.
losses: Kakatiya kingdom annexed.
outcomes: Warangal renamed Sultanpur; Musunuri Nayakas and Reddis rose.

events.title: Muhammad-bin-Tughlaq's experiments
events.summary: Muhammad bin Tughlaq (1325–1351) tries bold plans — moving the capital to Daulatabad, token currency and the Khurasan army — which fail (NCERT).
events.detail:
NCERT explains: to face the Mongols he raised a huge standing army and, instead of building a new garrison town, emptied the oldest city, Delhi, sending people to Daulatabad in the south (1327). He paid the army with token currency of cheap metal, which people forged easily. The army raised for the Khurasan campaign was disbanded. Famine and rebellions followed.

Ibn Battuta served as qazi of Delhi under him (NCERT). In the south Vijayanagara (1336) and the Bahmanis (1347) rose during his reign.
causes: Mongol threat; plans to rule the south (NCERT).
outcomes: Rebellions; Vijayanagara and Bahmani kingdoms rose.

events.title: Reddi kingdoms rise in coastal Andhra
events.summary: After the Kakatiya fall, Prolaya Vema Reddi founds the Reddi kingdom in coastal Andhra (c. 1325) with capital Addanki, later Kondavidu and Rajahmundry.
events.detail: The Reddis repaired temples and tanks and patronised Telugu literature. Errana (Errapragada) completed the Telugu Mahabharata at Prolaya Vema's court; Srinatha was "Vidyadhikari" to Pedakomati Vema Reddi. The Reddis fought Vijayanagara, the Bahmanis, the Velamas of Rachakonda and the Gajapatis; Kondavidu fell to the Gajapatis (1448).
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
causes: Kakatiya fall (1323).
outcomes: Reddi rule until c. 1448.
events.yearHook: c. 1325 — two years after the Kakatiya fall.

participants.role: Court poet of the later Reddis.

facts: Reddi rule c. 1325–1448 CE. Kings: Prolaya Vema, Anavota, Anavema, Kumaragiri, Kataya Vema, Peda Komati Vema (Peda Komati Vema Reddy), Racha Vema.
Kondaveedu Fort was the Reddi stronghold; Anitalli was a Reddi queen (Kalayana grant); Ahobilam temple was patronised.
Srinatha was "Kavisarvabhauma".
Surambika, queen of Pedakomati Vema, dug the tank Santana Sagaram (APPSC Group-II 2018 key).
Vasantotsavam (spring festival) was the favourite festival under the Reddis (APPSC Group-II 2018 key).
Pedakomati Vema wrote "Sangita Chintamani" on music (APPSC Group-II 2018 key).
Reddi kings in order: Anavota Reddi, Anavema Reddi, Kumaragiri Reddi, Pedakomati Vema Reddi (after the founder Prolaya Vema) (APPSC Group-II 2025 key).
The Reddi king Racha Vema was notorious for heavy taxes, including Puriti Pannu (tax on the delivery of a child); he was killed by a servant (APPSC Group-II Screening 2018 key).

events.title: Musunuri Nayaks recapture Warangal
events.summary: The Musunuri Nayakas, Prolaya and Kapaya, lead Telugu chiefs in a revolt that frees coastal Andhra and Telangana from Tughlaq rule; Kapaya Nayaka captures Warangal (c. 1336).
events.detail: Prolaya Nayaka's Vilasa grant describes the suffering under Tughlaq rule and the liberation. Kapaya Nayaka ruled from Warangal and helped Hasan Gangu found the Bahmani kingdom (1347), but later lost Warangal to the Bahmanis and the Recherla Velamas (1368).
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
causes: Tughlaq oppression after 1323.
outcomes: Telugu rule restored; Reddis, Velamas and Vijayanagara rose.

participants.role: Founded the Bahmani kingdom with Kapaya's help.

facts: Recherla Velamas ruled c. 1328–1482 in Telangana.

events.title: Vijayanagara Empire founded
events.summary: Two brothers, Harihara and Bukka, found the Vijayanagara empire on the Tungabhadra in 1336 (NCERT); the Sangama dynasty rules till 1485 (NCERT).
events.detail:
They had served the Kakatiyas or Kampili, by tradition; the sage Vidyaranya is said to have inspired them. The capital Vijayanagara (Hampi) grew into a great walled city (NCERT). Dynasties: Sangama (till 1485), Saluva (till 1503), Tuluva and Aravidu (from 1542) (NCERT).

Rulers were called rayas; military chiefs called nayakas held land (amara) and supplied troops — the amara-nayaka system (NCERT). Ruins of Hampi were brought to light in 1800 by Colin Mackenzie (NCERT).
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History II, Ch. 7 "An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara"
causes: Weak Tughlaq control in the south.
outcomes: Vijayanagara–Bahmani wars for the Raichur doab (NCERT).

alsoOn.text: Saluva Narasimha replaces the Sangama dynasty (NCERT).
The Tuluvas replace the Saluvas (NCERT).
Colin Mackenzie surveys the ruins of Hampi (NCERT).

facts: Village officials: the ayagar system (12 village functionaries).
Vijayanagara rulers worshipped Virupaksha and Pampadevi at Hampi; later Vittala.
Fernao Nunes (Nuniz) was a Portuguese horse-trader who described the city.

events.title: Bahmani Sultanate founded in the Deccan
events.summary: Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah founds the Bahmani sultanate at Gulbarga (1347), the rival of Vijayanagara for the Raichur doab (NCERT).
events.detail:
The capital later moved to Bidar. Mahmud Gawan, the great minister, reformed the administration and built a madrasa at Bidar; his execution (1481) hastened the break-up.

By the early 16th century the kingdom split into five sultanates: Bijapur (Adil Shahi), Ahmadnagar (Nizam Shahi), Berar (Imad Shahi), Golconda (Qutb Shahi) and Bidar (Barid Shahi) (NCERT names the Deccan Sultanates).
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History II, Ch. 7 "An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara"; Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)
causes: Revolt of Deccan nobles against Muhammad bin Tughlaq.
outcomes: Five Deccan sultanates.

alsoOn.text: Mahmud Gawan executed; the Bahmani kingdom begins to break up.
Bijapur, Ahmadnagar and Berar become independent.

facts: The Bahmani kingdom was divided into 4, later 8 tarafs (provinces) under tarafdars.
Nobles were split into Afaqis (foreigners) and Deccanis (locals).
Five sultanates: Bijapur–Adil Shahi, Ahmednagar–Nizam Shahi, Berar–Imad Shahi, Golconda–Qutb Shahi, Bidar–Barid Shahi.
Sufi saint Gesu Daraz (Gulbarga); Dakhini Urdu developed; Ibrahim Rauza (Bijapur).

events.title: Firoz Shah Tughlaq — canals & welfare
events.summary: Firoz Shah Tughlaq (1351–1388) rules Delhi; he builds canals and towns, imposes jizya on brahmanas, sets up a department of slaves and moves two Ashokan pillars to Delhi.
events.detail: He gave iqtas as hereditary grants and abolished harsh taxes, keeping only four sanctioned by the Sharia. He founded Firozabad, Jaunpur and Hisar and the Diwan-i-Khairat (charity) and Diwan-i-Bandagan (slaves). He wrote his memoirs, Futuhat-i-Firozshahi.
causes: Weakness after Muhammad bin Tughlaq.
outcomes: Sultanate weakened by hereditary iqtas.

participants.role: His pillars were moved to Delhi.

events.title: Timur sacks Delhi
events.summary: Timur invades India and sacks Delhi in December 1398; the Tughlaq dynasty collapses and the Sayyids (1414) follow.
events.detail: Timur came from Samarkand, defeated Nasiruddin Mahmud Tughlaq and massacred many in Delhi. He left Khizr Khan as governor of Multan; Khizr Khan took Delhi in 1414 and founded the Sayyid dynasty (NCERT: 1414–1421). Babur was descended from Timur (NCERT).
losses: Delhi plundered; thousands killed.
outcomes: Sayyid dynasty from 1414 (NCERT).

alsoOn.text: Khizr Khan founds the Sayyid dynasty (NCERT).

events.title: Lodi dynasty; Sikandar founds Agra
events.summary: Bahlul Lodi founds the Lodi dynasty (1451), the first Afghan rulers of Delhi; Sikandar Lodi founds Agra (1504), and Ibrahim Lodi loses to Babur at Panipat (1526).
events.detail: Bahlul conquered the Sharqi kingdom of Jaunpur. Sikandar Lodi moved the capital to Agra and introduced a measuring rod (gaz-i-Sikandari). Ibrahim's quarrels with nobles made Daulat Khan Lodi and Alam Khan invite Babur.
causes: Decline of the Sayyids.
outcomes: First Battle of Panipat (1526).

events.title: Vasco da Gama reaches Calicut
events.summary: Vasco da Gama reaches Calicut on 20 May 1498, opening a sea route from Europe to India round the Cape of Good Hope (NCERT: "from 1498 other actors appeared").
events.detail: He was received by the Zamorin of Calicut. Pedro Alvares Cabral followed (1500), Francisco de Almeida became the first viceroy (1505) and Albuquerque took Goa (1510). The Portuguese competed with Arab traders for spices.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History II, Ch. 7 "An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara"; Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)
causes: European search for a sea route to the spice trade.
outcomes: Portuguese empire in the Indian Ocean; later Dutch, English and French companies.
events.yearHook: 1498 → Goa 1510 → Dutch 1605 → English 1611 on the Andhra coast.
facts: The Blue Water Policy (control of the seas rather than land) was the Portuguese policy of Francisco de Almeida (APPSC Group-II 2025 key).
The Portuguese introduced the tomato (and chilli, potato, cashew) to the Telugu land (APPSC Group-II 2025 key).

events.title: Krishnadevaraya — Vijayanagara zenith
events.summary: Krishnadevaraya of the Tuluva dynasty becomes king of Vijayanagara (1509–1529) (NCERT); he takes the Raichur doab (1512), subdues Odisha (1514) and defeats Bijapur (1520) (NCERT).
events.detail:
His reign was marked by expansion and consolidation (NCERT). He defeated the Gajapati Prataparudra of Odisha, took Kondavidu (1515) and Udayagiri, and married the Gajapati princess. He built the Vitthala and Hazara Rama temples and fine gopurams, and founded Nagalapuram (NCERT).

He wrote Amuktamalyada in Telugu, on statecraft (NCERT). Eight poets — the Ashtadiggajas, led by Allasani Peddana, with Tenali Ramakrishna, Nandi Thimmana and others — adorned his court. Domingo Paes described him (NCERT).
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History II, Ch. 7 "An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara"
causes: Strong Tuluva leadership.
course: 1510: wins over the Bahmani-successor sultans at Diwani.
1512: Raichur doab (NCERT).
1514: Odisha subdued (NCERT).
1515: Kondavidu captured.
1520: Battle of Raichur — Bijapur defeated (NCERT).
gains: Raichur doab, coastal Andhra up to the Krishna.
outcomes: Vijayanagara at its height (NCERT).

alsoOn.text: Krishnadevaraya acquires the Raichur doab (NCERT).
Orissa (Gajapatis) subdued (NCERT).
Bijapur defeated at Raichur (NCERT).

facts: His minister was Timmarusu ("Appaji"). He also wrote Jambavati Kalyanam in Sanskrit; raya gopurams (Rayagopurams) were his gateways.
Vijayanagara taxes: Navidadere — tax on barbers; Melivamsam — tax on ploughs; Manevana — house tax; Tudimeya — marriage tax (APPSC Group-1 key).
The Kandachara department of the Rayas dealt with military affairs (APPSC Group-II 2018 key).
The Porumamilla inscription (1369) gives 12 rules to be observed while building a tank (APPSC Group-II 2018 key).
Vipra Vinodins were Brahmin jugglers who gave indoor entertainment (APPSC Group-II 2018 key).
Art critics rate the gopuras of the Tadipatri temple (Chintala Venkataramana) as the most beautiful in Andhra (APPSC Group-II 2018 key).
Krishnadevaraya set up a pillar of victory at Potnuru (near Vizianagaram) to mark his conquest of coastal Andhra (APPSC Group-II 2025 key).

events.title: Qutb Shahi dynasty founded at Golconda
events.summary: Sultan Quli, Bahmani governor of Telangana, declares independence and founds the Qutb Shahi dynasty of Golconda (1518).
events.detail: Golconda fort was rebuilt from a Kakatiya mud fort. The Qutb Shahis were Shia rulers who patronised Telugu as well as Persian and Dakhni. Ibrahim Qutb Shah (1550–1580), who had lived at Vijayanagara, was praised by Telugu poets as "Malki Bharama". Golconda was famous for diamonds from the Kollur mines.
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
causes: Break-up of the Bahmani kingdom.
outcomes: Qutb Shahi rule till 1687; Hyderabad founded (1591).
facts: The Qutb Shahis (1518–1687 CE) were of Turkoman descent.
Their buildings used granite and lime mortar in an Indo-Persian style (later British buildings in Hyderabad are Indo-Saracenic).
Ibrahim was called Malkibhirama (Malki Bharama).

events.title: First Battle of Panipat; Babur founds Mughal rule
events.summary: Babur defeats Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat (21 April 1526) and founds the Mughal empire (NCERT).
events.detail: Babur, ruler of Kabul (seized 1504) (NCERT), had a smaller army but used field guns under Ustad Ali and Mustafa and the tulughma (flanking) tactic, with carts tied together (araba). Ibrahim Lodi was killed. Babur captured Delhi and Agra (NCERT).
causes: Ibrahim Lodi's unpopularity; invitation by Daulat Khan Lodi.
losses: Ibrahim Lodi killed.
gains: Delhi and Agra for Babur (NCERT).
outcomes: Mughal empire founded (NCERT).

events.title: Battle of Khanwa — Babur defeats Rana Sanga
events.summary: Babur defeats the Rajput confederacy under Rana Sanga of Mewar at Khanwa (1527).
events.detail: Babur declared it a jihad and gave up wine before the battle. Guns again decided the result. In 1528 he took Chanderi from Medini Rai, and in 1529 defeated the Afghans at Ghaghra.
causes: Rana Sanga hoped Babur would leave India.
outcomes: Rajput power checked; Mughals settled in India.

alsoOn.text: Babur defeats the Afghans at Ghaghra.

events.title: Vijayanagara after Krishnadevaraya
events.summary: Krishnadevaraya dies in 1529; strain shows within the empire (NCERT), and by 1542 power shifts to the Aravidu family, with Rama Raya as regent.
events.detail: His half-brother Achyuta Deva Raya succeeded him. After Achyuta, the young Sadashiva Raya was king in name, while Aliya Rama Raya, Krishnadevaraya's son-in-law, held real power and played the Deccan sultans against one another (NCERT).
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History II, Ch. 7 "An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara"
causes: Succession disputes (NCERT).
outcomes: Aravidu control from 1542 (NCERT); Talikota 1565.

alsoOn.text: Control at the centre shifts to the Aravidu lineage (NCERT).

events.title: Lepakshi Veerabhadra temple (Vijayanagara)
events.summary: The Veerabhadra temple at Lepakshi (Anantapur) is built (c. 1530) by the brothers Virupanna and Viranna, governors under Achyuta Deva Raya; it is famous for its murals, a hanging pillar and a huge monolithic Nandi.
events.detail:
A high point of Vijayanagara art in Rayalaseema.

**Exam hooks:** Lepakshi mural ceilings; the "hanging pillar".
causes: Vijayanagara patronage.
outcomes: Lepakshi murals are a high point of Vijayanagara painting.

events.title: Sher Shah Suri interrupts Mughal rule
events.summary: Sher Shah Suri defeats Humayun at Chausa (1539) and Kanauj (1540) and rules Delhi (1540–1545); Humayun flees to Iran (NCERT).
events.detail:
Sher Shah, an Afghan of Bihar, introduced the silver rupiya, rebuilt the Grand Trunk Road with sarais, set up dak chaukis and measured land for revenue. NCERT notes that his administration was taken up and consolidated by Akbar. He built the Purana Qila in Delhi and his tomb at Sasaram.

Humayun took refuge with the Safavid Shah, and recaptured Delhi in 1555 (NCERT).
causes: Afghan revival in Bihar and Bengal.
outcomes: Sur rule 1540–1555; Humayun returned in 1555 (NCERT).

alsoOn.text: Battle of Chausa: Sher Shah defeats Humayun.
Humayun recaptures Delhi (NCERT).

facts: Sher Shah's land revenue: land classified into three categories (good, middle, bad) by produce, measured by a uniform system (gaz-i-Sikandari, jarib); one-third of the average produce taken as tax — not one-fourth (APPSC Group-1 key).
His Grand Trunk Road (Sadak-e-Azam) ran from Sonargaon (Bengal) to the Indus (Peshawar) (APPSC Group-1 key).

Battle of Chausa (1539) and Bilgram/Kannauj (1540) were fought between Humayun and Sher Shah — not by Jahangir; Khanwa (1527) was Babur's, Haldighati (1576) Akbar's (via Man Singh) (APPSC Group-II 2023 key).

events.title: Second Battle of Panipat; Akbar's reign secured
events.summary: Bairam Khan, regent of the 13-year-old Akbar, defeats Hemu at the Second Battle of Panipat (5 November 1556), securing the Mughal throne.
events.detail: Humayun died early in 1556. Hemu, the Hindu general and minister of the Sur ruler Adil Shah, captured Agra and Delhi and took the title Vikramaditya. At Panipat an arrow hit Hemu in the eye; his army broke, and he was captured and killed. Bairam Khan ruled as regent till 1560.
causes: Humayun's death; Hemu's capture of Delhi.
losses: Hemu killed.
outcomes: Akbar's rule secured.

events.title: Battle of Talikota (Rakshasi-Tangadi)
events.summary: At Rakshasi-Tangadi (Talikota), 23 January 1565, the combined armies of Bijapur, Ahmadnagar and Golconda rout Vijayanagara's army under Rama Raya; the capital is sacked and deserted (NCERT).
events.detail: Rama Raya had played the sultans against one another, which made them unite (NCERT). He was captured and beheaded. The city was looted for months (NCERT). The Aravidu rulers moved to Penukonda and later Chandragiri. Berar did not take part.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History II, Ch. 7 "An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara"
causes: Rama Raya's interference in the sultans' affairs (NCERT).
losses: Rama Raya killed; the city sacked (NCERT).
outcomes: Vijayanagara declined; capitals at Penukonda and Chandragiri.
facts: Aravidu rulers moved to Penukonda and Chandragiri; Venkatapati Raya II (Venkata II) allowed the Jesuits to build churches at Nellore and Chandragiri (APPSC Group-1 key).

events.title: Akbar proclaims Din-i-Ilahi & Sulh-i-Kul
events.summary: Akbar's policy of sulh-i kul (universal peace) leads in 1582 to the Din-i Ilahi (Tauhid-i Ilahi), a small circle of disciples; the mansabdari and zabt systems run his empire (NCERT).
events.detail:
Mansabdars held ranks (zat for pay and status, sawar for cavalry) and were paid through jagirs (NCERT). Todar Mal surveyed crop yields and prices for ten years to fix cash taxes — the zabt system (NCERT). The empire was divided into subas under subadars (NCERT).

Abul Fazl's Akbarnama and Ain-i Akbari record the reign (NCERT). Birbal was among the few members of the Din-i Ilahi.
causes: Ibadat Khana debates (NCERT).
outcomes: A tolerant state; system used by later Mughals (NCERT).
facts: Revenue: Zabti (zabt) and the Dahsala (ten-year average) system; peasants gave a kabuliyat (agreement) and received a patta.
Chittorgarh fell in 1568; Rohtasgarh fort was taken.
Babur wrote in Chagatai Turkish; the Mughals were Timurid and Chinggisid.

Revenue officials: Amalguzar — revenue collector in charge of a district; Karkuns — prepared the seasonal crop statistics; Qanungo — kept records of revenue payable by villages; Bitikchi — accountant (APPSC Group-1 key).

events.title: Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah founds Hyderabad
events.summary: Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah founds Hyderabad on the Musi (1591) and builds the Charminar at its centre.
events.detail: The city was planned on a grid with the Charminar, four arches (Char Kaman) and markets. Legend links its old name Bhagyanagar to his beloved Bhagmati. He was the first poet to compile a diwan in Dakhni Urdu. The Mecca Masjid was begun later (1617).
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
causes: Overcrowding of Golconda fort.
outcomes: Hyderabad became the capital of the Qutb Shahis and later the Nizams.

events.title: Kondapalli toys & Andhra crafts (GI)
events.summary: Kondapalli near Vijayawada becomes famous for light wooden toys made from tella poniki wood; with Machilipatnam Kalamkari and Etikoppaka toys they are among Andhra's GI crafts.
events.detail:
Handicraft heritage of coastal Andhra.

**Exam hooks:** GI tags — Kondapalli toys, Machilipatnam Kalamkari, Etikoppaka.
causes: Artisan settlements (Aryakshatriya craftsmen) at Kondapalli.
outcomes: GI tags in the 2000s.

events.title: Kuchipudi — classical dance of Andhra
events.summary: Kuchipudi, the classical dance of Andhra, grows from the dance-dramas of Kuchipudi village (Krishna district), shaped by Siddhendra Yogi (by tradition, 17th century).
events.detail: Siddhendra Yogi composed Bhama Kalapam. By tradition the Qutb Shahi ruler Abul Hasan Tana Shah granted the village to the performers (1678). It is one of India's eight classical dances.
causes: Bhakti dance-drama tradition.
outcomes: Recognised classical dance.
facts: Bhamakalapam is the signature Kuchipudi dance-drama; it combines lasya (graceful) and tandava (vigorous) elements.
Kuravanji is a dance-drama (gypsy fortune-teller theme) of the Tamil-Telugu south; Rukmini Devi Arundale (Kalakshetra, 1936) was its famous performer and reviver (APPSC Group-II Screening 2018 key).

events.title: English East India Company chartered
events.summary: Queen Elizabeth I grants a charter to the English East India Company on 31 December 1600, with a monopoly of trade with the East (NCERT).
events.detail: NCERT explains that the charter gave the Company the sole right to trade with the East, so no other English company could compete. The Dutch East India Company followed in 1602 and the French in 1664 (NCERT). The English first traded at Masulipatnam (1611) and Surat (1613).
events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 2 "From Trade to Territory"
causes: Profits of the spice trade.
outcomes: English factories at Masulipatnam (1611), Surat (1613), Madras (1639) and Calcutta (1690).
facts: Charter dated 31 Dec 1600. Main goods: cotton, silk, indigo, saltpetre, spices and later opium.
The Danish came to Tranquebar 1620 and Serampore; the Dutch at Chinsura; the English defeated the Dutch at the Battle of Bedara 1759.
French settlements in order: Surat (1668), Masulipatnam (1669), Pondicherry (1673–74), Chandernagore (1690), Yanam (1723), Mahe (1725), Karaikal (1739) (APPSC Group-1 key).
The French lost Pondicherry to the Dutch (1693) and got it back in 1697 by the Treaty of Ryswick (APPSC Group-1 key).
Yanam was the French settlement in Andhra (APPSC Group-II 2025 key).

events.title: Jahangir's reign; English embassy
events.summary: Jahangir (Prince Salim) becomes Mughal emperor (1605–1627); in 1611 he marries Mehrunnisa, who becomes Nur Jahan (NCERT).
events.detail: He hung a chain of justice at Agra fort. He executed Guru Arjan (1606), received Hawkins and Sir Thomas Roe, and lost Kandahar to Iran (1622). Nur Jahan issued coins and orders; her family dominated the court (NCERT). Mughal painting flourished under Abul Hasan and Mansur.
causes: Akbar's death (1605).
outcomes: Nur Jahan's influence (NCERT).

alsoOn.text: Jahangir marries Mehrunnisa, who receives the title Nur Jahan (NCERT).

events.title: European factories at Masulipatnam (Andhra coast)
events.summary: The English set up their first factory on the east coast at Masulipatnam (Machilipatnam) in 1611, in the Golconda kingdom; the Dutch had come there in 1605.
events.detail: The ship Globe arrived under Captain Hippon. Masulipatnam exported calico (machilipatnam cloth) and Kalamkari to Southeast Asia and Europe. The English moved their main base to Madras (1639–41). The French also came (1669).
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
causes: Textile trade of the Golconda coast.
outcomes: Masulipatnam became a key port until Madras grew.

pairs.left: First English factory on the east coast

alsoOn.text: Dutch factory at Masulipatnam.

facts: The Globe reached Machilipatnam in 1611 under Captain Hippon, not Hawkins; the Qutb Shah permitted the English factory there (APPSC Group-II 2025 key).
The English set up their first factory in coastal Andhra at Machilipatnam (APPSC Group-II 2025 key).
Narsapur (Narasapuram, West Godavari) was the main ship-building centre of coastal Andhra in the 16th-17th centuries; the Dutch also built ships there (APPSC Group-II Screening 2018 key).

events.title: Shah Jahan; the Taj Mahal
events.summary: Shah Jahan (Prince Khurram) becomes Mughal emperor (1628–1658), the age of the Taj Mahal, the Red Fort and the Peacock Throne (NCERT).
events.detail: He annexed Ahmadnagar (1633) and made Bijapur and Golconda accept Mughal overlordship (1636). He moved the capital to Shahjahanabad (1648). In 1657 he fell ill; his sons fought for the throne and Aurangzeb imprisoned him in Agra fort, where he died in 1666.
causes: Jahangir's death.
outcomes: Mughal architecture at its peak (NCERT).

events.title: Aurangzeb; Mughal empire at its largest
events.summary: Aurangzeb wins the war of succession — defeating Dara Shukoh at Samugarh (1658) — imprisons Shah Jahan and becomes emperor (1658–1707) (NCERT).
events.detail: He executed his brothers Dara, Shuja and Murad. The empire reached its largest size: he annexed Bijapur (1686) and Golconda (1687) (NCERT). But revolts by Jats, Satnamis, Sikhs, Rajputs and Marathas, and 25 years of war in the Deccan, exhausted the treasury (NCERT). He reimposed jizya (1679).
causes: Shah Jahan's illness (1657); war of succession.
outcomes: Mughal empire at its widest; long Deccan wars (NCERT).

alsoOn.text: Aurangzeb reimposes jizya.

events.title: Shivaji crowned; Maratha state rises
events.summary: Shivaji is crowned Chhatrapati at Raigad (1674), founding the Maratha kingdom (NCERT).
events.detail:
Born at Shivneri in 1630 to Shahji and Jija Bai, Shivaji carved out a kingdom with the help of deshmukhs and peasant-pastoralists (NCERT). He killed Afzal Khan of Bijapur (1659), raided Surat (1664), signed the Treaty of Purandar (1665) and escaped from Agra (1666).

He was helped by a council of eight ministers, the Ashtapradhan, headed by the Peshwa. After his death in 1680, Sambhaji, Rajaram and Tarabai continued the fight against Aurangzeb (NCERT).
causes: Weakness of Bijapur; Maratha deshmukh support (NCERT).
outcomes: Maratha state; the Peshwas later expanded it (NCERT).

alsoOn.text: Shivaji born at Shivneri (NCERT).
Shivaji kills Afzal Khan of Bijapur at Pratapgad.
Shivaji dies; Sambhaji succeeds (NCERT).

facts: Ashtapradhan: Peshwa (prime minister), Amatya/Majumdar (finance), Mantri/Waqia-navis (records, intelligence, household), Sachiv/Surunavis (correspondence), Sumant/Dabir (master of ceremonies, foreign affairs), Senapati (army), Panditrao (religious grants), Nyayadhish (justice) (APPSC Group-1 key).

In Shivaji's Ashtapradhan the Senapati was also called Sar-i-Naubat (commander-in-chief); Peshwa = Mukhya Pradhan, Amatya/Majumdar = finance, Sachiv/Surunavis = correspondence, Mantri/Waqia-navis = records, Sumant/Dabir = foreign affairs, Nyayadhish = justice, Panditrao = religion (APPSC Group-II 2023 key).

events.title: Aurangzeb annexes Golconda
events.summary: Aurangzeb captures Golconda (1687) after an eight-month siege, ending the Qutb Shahi dynasty; Abul Hasan Tana Shah is imprisoned at Daulatabad.
events.detail: Tana Shah's Brahmin ministers Madanna and Akkanna had allied with Shivaji (1677); they were murdered in 1686. The fort fell when a noble, Abdullah Khan Pani, opened a gate. Bhakta Ramadasu (Kancherla Gopanna), tahsildar of Bhadrachalam and nephew of Madanna, is remembered from this time. Golconda became a Mughal suba of the Deccan.
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
causes: Golconda's alliance with the Marathas; Aurangzeb's Deccan policy.
losses: Qutb Shahi kingdom annexed.
outcomes: Golconda a Mughal province; later part of the Nizam's state (1724).

alsoOn.text: Aurangzeb annexes Bijapur.

events.title: Asaf Jahi Nizams found Hyderabad State
events.summary: Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah I defeats the Mughal governor Mubariz Khan at Shakar Kheda (1724) and rules the Deccan as virtually independent — the start of the Nizams of Hyderabad (NCERT).
events.detail: NCERT says he was entrusted with the governorship of the Deccan and became its effective ruler, bringing skilled soldiers and administrators from north India, while never formally breaking with the emperor. The capital later moved from Aurangabad to Hyderabad (1763). The Asaf Jahi dynasty ruled until 1948.
causes: Weak Mughal centre after 1707 (NCERT).
outcomes: Hyderabad State till 1948.

events.title: Carnatic Wars (Anglo-French rivalry)
events.summary: The First Carnatic War (1746–48) begins when the French under Dupleix take Madras; at Adyar a small French force defeats the Nawab of Arcot's large army. The Second (1749–54) and Third (1756–63) wars follow, and the English win.
events.detail:
The wars were an extension of the Anglo-French conflict in Europe (War of Austrian Succession). La Bourdonnais captured Madras (1746); the Nawab Anwaruddin sent his son Mahfuz Khan, whose army was routed by Paradis at the Battle of Adyar (St Thome). The Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle (1748) returned Madras to the English.

In the Second War the French backed Chanda Sahib (Carnatic) and Muzaffar Jang (Hyderabad), the English backed Muhammad Ali; Robert Clive's capture and defence of Arcot (1751) turned the tide; Dupleix was recalled (1754). Bussy, posted at Hyderabad, got the Northern Circars for the French (1753). The Third War ended at Wandiwash (1760) and the Treaty of Paris (1763).
events.source: Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)
causes: Anglo-French rivalry in Europe and India.
Succession disputes in the Carnatic and Hyderabad.
course: 1746: French take Madras; Battle of Adyar.
1748: Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle.
1751: Clive takes Arcot.
1753: Northern Circars to the French via Bussy.
1754: Dupleix recalled; Treaty of Pondicherry.
1760: Wandiwash; 1763: Treaty of Paris.

treaties.name: Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle
terms: Madras returned to the English.

treaties.name: Treaty of Pondicherry
terms: Both agreed not to interfere in Indian princes' quarrels.

outcomes: Showed that small European armies could beat large Indian armies.
English supremacy in the south after Wandiwash (1760).

alsoOn.text: Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle returns Madras to the English.
Robert Clive captures and holds Arcot.
Dupleix recalled; Treaty of Pondicherry.

facts: Treaty of Yandabo (1826) ended the First Anglo-Burmese War, not a Carnatic war; First Carnatic War ended by Aix-la-Chapelle (1748), Second by the Treaty of Pondicherry (1754), Third by the Treaty of Paris (1763) (APPSC Group-II 2023 key).

events.title: Battle of Plassey
events.summary: Clive defeats Siraj-ud-Daulah via Mir Jafar's treachery — Company power in Bengal.
events.detail:
In 1756 the new Nawab Sirajuddaulah, angry at the Company's fortifications and misuse of trade passes, seized its factory at Kassimbazar and Fort William in Calcutta. The Company sent Robert Clive from Madras. Clive won over Mir Jafar, one of the Nawab's commanders, by promising to make him nawab.

On 23 June 1757 the armies met at Plassey (Palashi). Mir Jafar's troops never fought, and Sirajuddaulah was crushed. It was the Company's first major victory in India.
events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 2 "From Trade to Territory" and Ch. 3 "Ruling the Countryside"; Standard modern Indian history (Spectrum / Bipan Chandra); NCERT Class 8 Ch. 2–3
events.place: Plassey (Palashi), on the Bhagirathi in Nadia district, Bengal
parties: Sirajuddaulah, Nawab of Bengal (with French help)
outcomes: Sirajuddaulah was assassinated; Mir Jafar was made nawab.
The Company got the zamindari of the 24 Parganas and huge payments.
Start of the Company's political power in Bengal.

participants.role: Retook Calcutta, made the secret deal with Mir Jafar, and led the Company army at Plassey.
Attacked the Company in 1756; lost at Plassey; caught and killed soon after.
The Nawab's commander; kept his troops out of the battle and was made nawab as his reward.
Siraj's grandfather; his death in 1756 brought Siraj to the throne.

facts: Battle of Plassey: 23 June 1757.
Plassey is the anglicised name of Palashi, named after the palash tree (NCERT).
It was the first major victory the Company won in India (NCERT).
Mir Jafar's forces never fought — the main reason for the Nawab's defeat (NCERT).
Plassey gave the Company political power; Buxar (1764) confirmed it.

alsoOn.text: Sirajuddaulah seizes the Company's factory at Kassimbazar and Fort William, Calcutta.

sides.name: East India Company
sides.ruler: Court of Directors, London (in Bengal: Robert Clive)

causes: The Company fortified Calcutta without the Nawab's permission and refused to stop (NCERT).
Company officials misused the duty-free trade passes (dastaks), cutting the Nawab's revenue (NCERT).
The Company tried to help one of Sirajuddaulah's rivals become nawab (NCERT).
In 1756 Sirajuddaulah seized the Company's factory at Kassimbazar and captured Fort William, Calcutta.
Clive and Admiral Watson came from Madras, retook Calcutta (January 1757) and seized French Chandernagore (March 1757).
Clive plotted with Mir Jafar, the banker Jagat Seth and others to replace the Nawab.

Heavy rain soaked the Nawab's gunpowder; the Company had covered its own.
The Nawab's loyal commander Mir Madan was killed early in the fighting.
Mir Jafar and the troops under him stood aside and never fought (NCERT).
Sirajuddaulah fled to Murshidabad; he was caught and killed by Mir Jafar's son Miran.

Nawab: about 500 killed; he lost his throne and his life.
gains: Mir Jafar became Nawab of Bengal.
The Company got the zamindari of the 24 Parganas and huge payments; Clive got a personal jagir.
The French in Bengal were finished.

treaties.name: Treaty of Alinagar

The Nawab restored the Company's trade privileges.
The Company could fortify Calcutta and mint coins.

treaties.name: Secret agreement with Mir Jafar

He would pay the Company and its officers large sums.

events.yearHook: Exactly 100 years before the Revolt of 1857: 1857 − 100 = 1757.

events.title: Industrial Revolution
events.summary: Mechanised production in Britain reshapes the global economy.
events.detail: The Industrial Revolution began in Britain about 1760 with machines for spinning and weaving (Hargreaves's spinning jenny 1764, Arkwright's water frame 1769, Cartwright's power loom 1785) and James Watt's steam engine (1769). NCERT explains that British factory cloth then flooded India, ruining Indian weavers, while India became a supplier of raw cotton and indigo.
causes: Capital from trade and colonies; coal and iron; new inventions.
outcomes: Decline of Indian handloom weaving (NCERT).
India became a market for British goods and a source of raw materials (NCERT).

events.title: Third Battle of Panipat
events.summary: Ahmad Shah Abdali of Afghanistan crushes the Maratha army under Sadashivrao Bhau on 14 January 1761.
events.detail:
The Mughal empire was too weak to defend north India. Two outside powers wanted control of it: the **Marathas**, who had spread their power up to the Punjab, and **Ahmad Shah Abdali**, the Afghan ruler, who invaded north India five times between 1748 and 1761 (NCERT).

The two armies faced each other at Panipat for about two months. Cut off from food, the starving Maratha army attacked on 14 January 1761 and was destroyed. The Marathas' dream of ruling from Delhi was shattered (NCERT).
events.source: NCERT Class 7 Our Pasts II, Ch. 8 "Eighteenth-Century Political Formations"; NCERT Class 8 Ch. 2
events.place: Panipat, about 90 km north of Delhi (Haryana)

sides.name: Marathas
sides.ruler: Peshwa Balaji Baji Rao (Nanasaheb), at Pune — on behalf of Chhatrapati Rajaram II
allies: No major Indian ally — the Jats (Suraj Mal) left the camp; Rajputs and Sikhs stayed away

sides.name: Afghans and allies
sides.ruler: Ahmad Shah Abdali (Durrani), King of Afghanistan

causes: The Mughal emperor was powerless; whoever controlled Delhi and the Punjab controlled north India.
Maratha expansion: in 1758 Raghunathrao took Lahore and drove out Abdali's son Timur Shah — a direct challenge to Abdali.
Abdali regarded the Punjab as his own after his earlier invasions.
Najib-ud-Daula, the Rohilla chief, feared the Marathas and invited Abdali to return.
In January 1760 Abdali killed the Maratha general Dattaji Sindhia at Barari Ghat near Delhi.
The Peshwa sent a large army north under Sadashivrao Bhau to restore Maratha power.
Maratha raids and tribute demands had made other rulers hostile, so they did not help (NCERT).
course: March 1760: Sadashivrao Bhau leaves the Deccan with the Peshwa's son Vishwasrao and a large army and camp.
August 1760: the Marathas capture Delhi.
October 1760: they storm Kunjpura, an Afghan post on the Yamuna.
Abdali crosses the Yamuna at Baghpat and gets between the Marathas and Delhi.
November 1760 – January 1761: both armies dig in at Panipat; Abdali cuts off Maratha food supplies. Govind Pant Bundele, sent to bring supplies, is killed.
14 January 1761: the starving Marathas attack at dawn. Ibrahim Khan Gardi's guns do great damage at first.
Around midday Vishwasrao is shot dead. Bhau charges into the fight and is killed.
Malhar Rao Holkar withdraws; the Maratha army breaks and is routed.
losses: Marathas: Sadashivrao Bhau, Vishwasrao, Jankoji Sindhia and Tukoji Sindhia killed; Ibrahim Khan Gardi captured and executed.
Tens of thousands of Maratha soldiers and camp followers killed or captured.
Mahadji Sindhia was badly wounded and lamed for life.
Afghans: heavy losses too; Abdali's soldiers refused to stay in India and he went home.
gains: Abdali won the battle but did not stay — he returned to Afghanistan in 1761.
He recognised Shah Alam II as Mughal emperor; Najib-ud-Daula held Delhi as Mir Bakhshi and Shuja-ud-Daula was named wazir.
The Company gained most: its two biggest Indian rivals for the north were weakened just as it rose in Bengal.
The Sikhs took over the Punjab in the years after.
outcomes: Maratha expansion in the north was checked for about ten years.
Peshwa Balaji Baji Rao died of shock in June 1761; Madhavrao I became Peshwa and rebuilt Maratha power.
The Maratha confederacy split into chiefs (Sindhia, Holkar, Gaikwad, Bhonsle) under the Peshwa (NCERT).
By 1771–72 Mahadji Sindhia brought Shah Alam II back to Delhi under Maratha protection.

participants.role: Invaded India, blockaded the Marathas and won the battle; then went back to Afghanistan.

participants.post: Commander-in-chief of the northern campaign, appointed by the Peshwa (1760)
participants.role: Led the Maratha army; took Delhi and Kunjpura; killed in the battle.

participants.post: Peshwa's heir; nominal head of the army
participants.role: Killed by a shot around midday — his death broke Maratha morale.
Peshwa who sent the army north; was marching with help when he heard the news, and died of grief months later.
His French-trained gunners did great damage early in the battle; captured and executed.
Senior Maratha chief; withdrew from the field as the battle turned.
Fought in the battle and escaped badly wounded; later rebuilt Maratha power in the north.
Rohilla chief who invited Abdali and fought for him; afterwards held Delhi.
Nawab of Awadh; joined Abdali's side.
Mughal emperor in name, living away from Delhi; Abdali recognised him after the battle.

Abdali's wazir; commanded the Afghan centre.
His death at Barari Ghat (January 1760) made the Peshwa send Bhau north.
Became Peshwa after the disaster and rebuilt Maratha power.
Took Lahore in 1758 and drove out Abdali's son — one cause of the war.

facts: Third Battle of Panipat: 14 January 1761.
Ahmad Shah Abdali invaded north India five times between 1748 and 1761 (NCERT).
The Maratha commander was Sadashivrao Bhau; the Peshwa at the time was Balaji Baji Rao.
No peace treaty was signed after the battle.
Panipat saw three great battles: 1526 (Babur vs Ibrahim Lodi), 1556 (Akbar's army under Bairam Khan vs Hemu), 1761 (Abdali vs Marathas).

alsoOn.text: Ahmad Shah Abdali is chosen King of Afghanistan at Kandahar after Nadir Shah's murder; founds the Durrani empire.
Ahmad Shah Abdali's first invasion of north India.
Raghunathrao captures Lahore and drives out Abdali's son Timur Shah.
Dattaji Sindhia killed by Abdali at Barari Ghat (January); Bhau beats the Nizam at Udgir and marches north; Marathas take Delhi (August).

events.title: Battle of Buxar
events.summary: Company defeats the Mughal-Awadh-Bengal alliance; gains Diwani (1765).
events.detail:
Mir Qasim, made nawab in 1760, wanted real power and complained about Company servants misusing duty-free trade passes. War followed. He joined the Nawab of Awadh, Shuja-ud-daula, and the Mughal emperor, Shah Alam II.

At Buxar in Bihar, Hector Munro's Company army defeated all three. Mir Qasim fled, and Mir Jafar was put back as nawab.
events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 2 "From Trade to Territory" and Ch. 3 "Ruling the Countryside"; Standard modern Indian history (Spectrum / Bipan Chandra); NCERT Class 8 Ch. 2–3
events.place: Buxar, on the Ganga in Bihar
parties: Mir Qasim (Bengal), Shuja-ud-daula (Awadh) and Shah Alam II (Mughal emperor)
outcomes: Mir Qasim was driven out of Bengal; Mir Jafar was reinstalled (NCERT).
Plassey had been won by treachery; Buxar was won in open battle, so it confirmed Company power.

participants.role: Commanded the Company army and defeated all three allied armies.
Former nawab who formed the alliance; lost and fled, dying in poverty.
Nawab of Awadh; led the largest allied force and was defeated.
Mughal emperor; stayed back in the battle, then made terms with the Company.
Put back on the throne of Bengal after Mir Qasim fled.
Governor of Bengal during the war.

facts: Battle of Buxar: 22 October 1764.
Buxar defeated three Indian powers at once — Bengal, Awadh and the Mughal emperor.
The Company commander at Buxar was Hector Munro.

sides.name: Allied Indian powers
sides.ruler: Mir Qasim (Bengal), Shuja-ud-Daula (Awadh), Shah Alam II (Mughal emperor)

causes: Mir Qasim wanted to rule Bengal as a real nawab, not a puppet.
He objected to Company servants misusing dastaks; war broke out in 1763 (NCERT).
Beaten in Bengal, he fled to Awadh and formed an alliance with Shuja-ud-Daula and Shah Alam II.
course: 1764: the allies marched into Bihar.
22 October 1764: Hector Munro's army met them at Buxar on the Ganga.
The Company's disciplined infantry and artillery broke the much larger allied army in a few hours.
Shah Alam II kept away from the fighting and soon came over to the British.
Shuja-ud-Daula fled; he was beaten again at Kora (1765) and surrendered.

Allies: about 2,000 killed and their army scattered.

It won the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa by the Treaty of Allahabad (1765).

events.title: Northern Circars pass to the Company
events.summary: The coastal Andhra Circars pass to the English East India Company.
events.detail:
The Northern Circars were the coastal districts of Andhra from Ganjam to Guntur. After Buxar, Shah Alam II's grant (1765) and a treaty with the Nizam (1766) gave them to the Company, which paid the Nizam a yearly sum.

Guntur followed in 1788. In 1800 the Nizam also gave up the Rayalaseema districts — the 'Ceded Districts'. Together they formed British Andhra in the Madras Presidency.

Granted the Circars to the Company by a farman (1765).
Obtained the farman from the emperor.
French general who had held the Circars since 1753.

outcomes: Coastal Andhra came under the Madras Presidency.
With the Ceded Districts (1800), almost all of today's Andhra came under the Company.

1788: the Guntur Circar also passes to the Company.

events.title: Regulating Act, 1773
events.summary: The first Act of the British Parliament to control the Company's rule in India.
events.detail:
The British Parliament stepped in to control the Company's affairs in India.

- The Governor of Bengal became the Governor-General of Bengal, with a council of four.
- The Governors of Bombay and Madras were placed under him.
- A Supreme Court was set up at Calcutta (1774), with Sir Elijah Impey as the first Chief Justice.
- Company servants were barred from private trade and from taking gifts.
events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 2; standard constitutional history

Became the first Chief Justice of the new Supreme Court at Calcutta (1774).
One of the four councillors named in the Act; led the opposition to Hastings.

outcomes: Start of parliamentary control over the Company.
First step in India's constitutional development.
Its weaknesses — the Governor-General could be outvoted by his council — led to Pitt's India Act (1784).
facts: Passed under British Prime Minister Lord North.
Created the post of Governor-General of Bengal; Warren Hastings was the first.
Supreme Court at Calcutta (1774); first Chief Justice Sir Elijah Impey.
Council of four: Philip Francis, Clavering, Monson and Barwell.

The Company itself was nearly bankrupt and asked the government for a loan (1772).
Parliament decided the Company must be supervised.
course: 1773: Parliament passes the Act under Prime Minister Lord North.
The Governor of Bengal becomes Governor-General of Bengal, with a council of four.
The Governors of Bombay and Madras are placed under him in matters of war and peace.
1774: a Supreme Court is set up at Calcutta.

events.title: American Declaration of Independence
events.summary: Thirteen colonies declare independence from Britain.
events.detail: The thirteen American colonies declared independence from Britain on 4 July 1776; Thomas Jefferson drafted the Declaration. Britain lost the war (Treaty of Paris, 1783). Cornwallis, who surrendered at Yorktown (1781), was then sent to India as Governor-General (1786).
causes: "No taxation without representation."
outcomes: USA independent (1783).
Britain turned more firmly to India; Cornwallis came to India (1786).
events.yearHook: 1776 — the year after the Treaty of Surat (Marathas).

participants.role: Lost at Yorktown (1781); Governor-General of India from 1786.

events.title: French Revolution
events.summary: Liberty, Equality, Fraternity; fall of the Bastille begins modern republicanism.
events.detail: The French Revolution began with the storming of the Bastille on 14 July 1789, with the ideals of liberty, equality and fraternity. Its ideas inspired Tipu Sultan, who planted a "tree of liberty" at Srirangapatnam and joined a Jacobin club, and later Indian reformers such as Ram Mohan Roy.
causes: Royal debt, privilege of nobles and clergy, Enlightenment ideas.
outcomes: End of absolute monarchy in France; Napoleon's wars.
Liberty, equality, fraternity — words later in the Preamble of the Indian Constitution.
events.yearHook: 1789 — the year before the Third Mysore War.

events.title: Permanent Settlement of Bengal
events.summary: Cornwallis fixes land revenue with zamindars in perpetuity.
events.detail:
The Company wanted a steady revenue and hoped zamindars would invest in the land. Under Lord Cornwallis, the revenue was fixed permanently with the rajas and taluqdars, who were recognised as zamindars.

The zamindars collected rent from the peasants and paid the fixed amount to the Company. It soon created problems: the fixed revenue was very high, many zamindars lost their land when they failed to pay, and peasants paid rising rents.
events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 3 "Ruling the Countryside"

participants.role: Senior revenue official who planned it; later Governor-General.
Had argued for a fixed permanent revenue years earlier.

outcomes: Later officials found it too rigid — Ryotwari (Madras, from c. 1820) and Mahalwari (North-Western Provinces, 1822) followed (NCERT).
facts: Introduced by Lord Cornwallis in 1793.
Also called the Zamindari system.
The Mahalwari system was devised by Holt Mackenzie and came into effect in 1822 (North-Western Provinces).
The Ryotwari system was tried by Alexander Read and developed by Thomas Munro in the south.

Permanent Settlement: introduced by Cornwallis in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa in 1793 (not 1795); zamindars became owners with hereditary rights; John Shore planned it; the revenue was fixed for ever (APPSC Group-II 2023 key).

alsoOn.text: Holt Mackenzie's Mahalwari settlement comes into effect in the North-Western Provinces.

causes: Revenue from Bengal kept falling after the famine of 1770; the Company wanted a fixed, steady income (NCERT).
Earlier systems — auctioning collection rights to the highest bidder — had ruined both peasants and revenue.
Officials believed that if zamindars owned the land permanently, they would invest in improving it (NCERT).
course: 1789–90: a ten-year (decennial) settlement is made with the zamindars.
22 March 1793: Cornwallis declares it permanent.
The revenue fixed in 1793 could never be raised.
"Sunset law": a zamindar who did not pay by sunset on the due date lost his estate, which was auctioned (NCERT).
losses: Peasants: rents went up and they had no security.
Old zamindar families: many lost their estates at auctions (NCERT).
Company: later, it could not raise revenue even when production grew.
gains: Company: a fixed, assured revenue.
Zamindars: became owners of the land.
events.yearHook: Cornwallis fixed it for ever in 1793 — the same year as a Charter Act (every 20 years: 1793, 1813…).

events.title: Wellesley's Subsidiary Alliance system
events.summary: Rulers accept British troops & Resident in return for "protection".
events.detail:
Lord Wellesley used the Subsidiary Alliance to bring Indian states under Company control without war.

- The Indian ruler could not keep his own independent army.
- The Company would protect him, but he had to pay for the 'subsidiary force'.
- A British Resident lived at his court.
- If he failed to pay, part of his territory was taken as penalty.

participants.role: Governor-General who introduced the system in 1798.
Nawab of Awadh; ceded half his territory (1801).
Accepted it by the Treaty of Bassein (1802).
Boy ruler of Mysore placed on the throne under it (1799).

outcomes: Indian rulers lost control over their armies and foreign policy.
Awadh (1801) and Hyderabad (1800) were forced to cede territory for failing to pay.
facts: The Nizam of Hyderabad was the first to accept the Subsidiary Alliance (1798).
When Wellesley was Governor-General, Awadh was forced to give over half its territory (1801).

He feared the French — Napoleon was in Egypt (1798) and Tipu had French contacts.
Wars were costly; the alliance made Indian rulers pay for British troops.
